Fulbright scholarship eligibility and application steps

The Fulbright scholarship is one of the most competitive and prestigious awards available to international students. This section covers the core eligibility criteria, required documents and the step-by-step application timeline that every candidate must follow.

faq.q: Is the Fulbright scholarship fully funded?
faq.a: It depends on your country. Many Fulbright grants are full awards covering tuition support, a living stipend, airfare and health benefits, while some are partial and shared with the host university. Check your national program's specifics for the 2026–27 cycle.

faq.q: When do I apply for the 2026–27 Fulbright cycle?
faq.a: Most national programs open applications in the spring and close around May–June before the year you travel, but deadlines vary by country. Always confirm on your home country's Fulbright Commission or US Embassy page, and start your essays several months ahead.

faq.q: How do I apply for a Fulbright scholarship?
faq.a: You apply through the Fulbright Commission or US Embassy in your home country, not directly to the US government. Each country sets its own deadlines, priority fields and application portal.

faq.q: What is the two-year home-country requirement?
faq.a: Most Fulbright grantees must return to their home country for at least two years after the program before applying for certain US immigrant and work visas. It reflects Fulbright's mission of exchange and bringing knowledge home.

faq.q: What matters most in a Fulbright application?
faq.a: A specific, well-argued study or research objective in the Statement of Grant Purpose, a reflective Personal Statement, and a clear commitment to cultural exchange usually matter more than having a flawless CV.

posts.title: DAAD Scholarships: Fund Your Study in Germany
posts.metaDescription: A clear guide to the DAAD scholarship: programme types like EPOS, eligibility, funding, and how to apply to study or research in Germany with full support.
posts.excerpt: Understand the DAAD scholarship, from EPOS and study grants to research funding, plus eligibility, benefits, and a step-by-step application guide.
posts.bodyHtml:
If you want to study in Germany with financial support, the DAAD scholarship should be at the top of your list. DAAD, the German Academic Exchange Service, is the world's largest funding organisation for the international exchange of students and researchers, and each year a DAAD scholarship helps tens of thousands of people from around the globe study, research, and build their careers in Germany.

This guide explains what DAAD is, the main types of scholarships available, who is eligible, and how to put together a strong application. Germany combines world-class universities, strong industry links, and famously low or no tuition fees, and DAAD funding can cover the living costs that make studying there fully affordable.

Key takeaways

  • A DAAD scholarship typically funds master's, doctoral, and research stays in Germany with a monthly stipend and often insurance and travel allowances.
  • DAAD is not a single scholarship but an umbrella covering hundreds of programmes for different fields, levels, and countries.
  • Most well-known is the EPOS programme (Development-Related Postgraduate Courses) for professionals from developing countries.
  • Applications are usually field- and programme-specific, with deadlines often falling many months before study begins.
  • Because German public universities frequently charge little or no tuition, a DAAD stipend can make studying essentially cost-neutral.

What is DAAD?

The DAAD (Deutscher Akademischer Austauschdienst) is a joint organisation of German universities that promotes international academic exchange. It funds German students going abroad and international students and researchers coming to Germany. For most international readers, the relevant offer is a DAAD scholarship to study or research in Germany.

Crucially, DAAD is a gateway rather than a single award. Its scholarship database lists hundreds of programmes, each with its own eligibility rules, target countries, academic fields, and application requirements. The key to success is finding the specific programme that matches your profile.

Types of DAAD scholarships

Development-Related Postgraduate Courses (EPOS)

One of the best-known DAAD offers, EPOS funds master's and some PhD study for professionals from developing and emerging countries. It targets fields relevant to sustainable development, such as public policy, economics, engineering, agriculture, public health, and environmental management. EPOS awards are generous and typically fully funded, but they usually require a few years of relevant work experience.

Study Scholarships for graduates

These support international graduates who want to pursue a full master's degree, or in some cases a shorter study period, in Germany. They are open across many disciplines and are aimed at highly qualified students at the start of their postgraduate journey.

Research Grants for doctoral candidates

DAAD offers several formats for PhD study, including full doctoral programmes in Germany, short-term research stays, and cotutelle or binational arrangements. These grants suit early-career researchers who have identified a German supervisor or research group.

Subject-specific and country-specific programmes

Many DAAD programmes are tied to particular fields (such as music, fine art, or architecture) or to partnerships with specific countries and regions. This is why searching the official DAAD scholarship database with your own profile is essential.

To understand how DAAD compares with other funded routes into Europe, it can help to browse fully funded scholarships and shortlist the ones that fit your background.

What does a DAAD scholarship cover?

Benefits vary by programme, but a typical fully funded DAAD scholarship often includes:

  • A monthly stipend set at a level intended to cover living costs in Germany, usually higher for doctoral candidates than for master's students.
  • Health, accident, and liability insurance coverage.
  • A travel allowance or airfare contribution, depending on your programme and home country.
  • In many cases, additional support such as a study or research allowance, rent subsidies, family allowances, or a German language course before your studies begin.

Because tuition at German public universities is often free or limited to a small semester contribution, a DAAD stipend frequently means your studies are effectively fully funded.

DAAD eligibility: who can apply?

Eligibility is defined per programme, but common threads include:

  • A relevant completed degree (usually a bachelor's for master's scholarships, and a master's for doctoral funding).
  • A strong academic record and, for many programmes, graduation within the last few years.
  • Work experience, often around two years, for development-related programmes such as EPOS.
  • Language proficiency: English for English-taught programmes (TOEFL or IELTS), or German for German-taught courses.
  • Citizenship or residency in an eligible country for the specific programme.

Always read the individual programme page. Applying to a scholarship you are not eligible for is one of the most common wasted efforts.

How to apply for a DAAD scholarship, step by step

1. Search the DAAD scholarship database

Start on the official DAAD website and filter the scholarship database by your country, degree level, and subject. Make a shortlist of programmes for which you clearly qualify and note their deadlines, which often fall many months before the study start date.

2. Choose your German course or host

Depending on the programme, you may need to select from a defined list of participating courses (as with EPOS) or secure a supervisor for research funding. Choose programmes that match your academic and career goals, since consistency strengthens your application.

3. Prepare your documents

DAAD applications are document-heavy. You will typically need:

  • A completed DAAD application form.
  • A detailed CV, often in a specified Europass or DAAD format.
  • A motivation letter or statement of purpose tailored to your chosen programme.
  • For research grants, a research proposal and often a letter from a prospective supervisor.
  • Academic transcripts, degree certificates, and language certificates.
  • Letters of recommendation, and for work-related programmes, proof of employment.

4. Write a compelling motivation letter

Your motivation letter is where you connect your background, your chosen programme, and your future goals. Explain clearly why this specific course in Germany, why now, and how it fits your career plan, especially any development impact for programmes like EPOS. Our SOP builder can help you shape a focused, persuasive statement.

5. Submit and prepare for possible interviews

Some programmes involve an interview or additional selection stage. If shortlisted, be ready to discuss your goals, your proposed studies, and how you will apply your learning afterwards.

Tips for a strong DAAD application

Match your profile to the exact programme

Because DAAD is so varied, fit is everything. A modest profile that perfectly matches a niche programme often beats an impressive profile applying to the wrong one. Read each programme's aims and tailor your materials accordingly.

Show development relevance where required

For EPOS and similar awards, selectors want to see how your studies will contribute to sustainable development in your home country. Be concrete about the change you intend to make.

Be meticulous with documents

DAAD is known for detailed requirements and specific formats. Missing or incorrectly formatted documents can lead to rejection before your merits are even considered. Build a checklist and follow it exactly.

Get feedback before submitting

A second pair of eyes can catch weak arguments and unclear phrasing. Our AI advisor can review your motivation letter and research proposal to help you present your case clearly.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Treating DAAD as one scholarship. Always find the specific programme that fits you.
  • Ignoring work-experience requirements. Programmes like EPOS expect relevant professional experience.
  • Generic motivation letters. Tailor every application to the chosen course and its goals.
  • Overlooking language requirements. Check whether your programme needs German or English proof.
  • Missing early deadlines. DAAD deadlines often fall a year before study begins.

The DAAD application timeline

DAAD programmes are notorious for early deadlines, and missing them is a frequent, avoidable mistake. While each programme sets its own dates, a typical rhythm for a course starting in the autumn looks like this:

  • Roughly a year before: Search the database, shortlist programmes, and confirm eligibility and required documents.
  • Autumn to winter: Many EPOS and postgraduate deadlines fall in this window, often between late summer and the following spring depending on the course.
  • Months after the deadline: Shortlisting, possible interviews, and final decisions.
  • The following autumn: Your studies begin, sometimes preceded by a German language course.

Because DAAD requires detailed, sometimes certified documents and specific CV formats, give yourself at least a few months of preparation. Rushed applications with missing paperwork are commonly filtered out before assessment.

Understanding the selection criteria

DAAD selectors typically weigh your academic performance, the quality and relevance of your motivation letter or research proposal, your professional experience where required, and the fit between your goals and the programme's aims. For development-oriented awards like EPOS, the potential impact of your studies on your home country carries significant weight. Presenting a coherent story, from your background to your chosen course to your intended impact, is what separates strong applications from average ones.

Language preparation and integration

Even if your programme is taught in English, learning some German improves daily life, employability, and integration. DAAD sometimes funds a preparatory German language course before your studies begin, which is both practical and a sign that the programme values your successful adjustment. If your course is taught in German, plan your language certification (such as TestDaF or DSH) well in advance, as reaching the required level takes time.

Combining DAAD with Germany's low tuition

A major reason DAAD offers such strong value is the German higher education system itself. Because public universities generally charge little or no tuition, a DAAD stipend does not need to be stretched across large fees; it can be devoted almost entirely to living costs. This is fundamentally different from scholarships in high-tuition countries, where much of an award may be consumed by fees alone.

The practical upshot is that a fully funded DAAD scholarship can genuinely make your studies cost-neutral. When comparing offers, factor in this combination of low tuition and a living-cost stipend, because it can make a DAAD-funded degree more affordable overall than a nominally larger award elsewhere.

What if you are not selected?

It also helps to look beyond the best-known awards. Because DAAD is an umbrella for hundreds of programmes, there are often less crowded, highly specific opportunities tied to particular subjects, regions, or partnerships that match a narrow profile very well. Spending extra time in the scholarship database to find these niche programmes can meaningfully improve your odds compared with applying only to the most famous schemes.

DAAD is competitive, and many strong candidates apply more than once or to more than one programme. If you are not selected, seek to understand where your application was weakest, whether that was the motivation letter, the match to the programme, or your documentation. You can also explore other funding routes and university-level scholarships in parallel. Persistence, combined with a genuinely well-matched application, pays off for many DAAD applicants over time. Keep records of your applications and any feedback, and treat each attempt as a chance to sharpen your motivation letter and clarify your goals.

Why Germany plus DAAD is a powerful combination

Working and living in Germany as a DAAD scholar

A DAAD stipend is designed to cover your living costs, so you can focus on your studies rather than juggling part-time work. That said, understanding the practicalities of student life in Germany helps you settle quickly. You will need to register your address after arrival, open a local bank account, and arrange the mandatory health insurance that DAAD often supports. University towns are generally welcoming to international students, and the semester ticket that comes with many enrolments makes getting around affordable.

Germany also offers strong links between universities and industry, particularly at universities of applied sciences. Many programmes include internships or project work with companies, which can be invaluable for your career, especially in engineering, technology, and business fields. As a DAAD scholar, engaging with these opportunities strengthens both your learning and your professional network.

Career prospects after a DAAD-funded degree

A degree from a respected German university, combined with the prestige of a DAAD scholarship, is a strong foundation for your career. For development-oriented programmes, the expectation is that you will return home and apply your expertise, and DAAD values this contribution highly. For other programmes, Germany's post-study landscape can offer opportunities to gain experience, subject to visa rules and your programme's terms. Either way, the international network you build as a DAAD scholar, including fellow scholars and alumni around the world, is a lasting professional asset.

Why Germany plus DAAD is a powerful combination for value

To appreciate the full value of a DAAD scholarship, it helps to see it alongside the broader German system. Because public universities generally charge little or no tuition, your stipend is not eroded by fees, and the overall cost of a high-quality education is remarkably low. Few countries combine world-class institutions, strong industry ties, and this level of affordability. When you add a fully funded scholarship on top, the result is a genuinely rare opportunity to study and grow without the heavy debt that graduate study can involve elsewhere.

Germany offers globally respected universities, strong ties to industry and research, and a high quality of life, often with little or no tuition at public institutions. Add a DAAD scholarship to cover living costs, and you have a route to a fully funded, high-value education. With careful programme selection and a well-crafted application, DAAD can open the door to your studies in Germany and to a valuable international network for the rest of your career.

DAAD scholarship interview preparation and common questions

Many DAAD scholarship programmes include an interview as a key stage in the selection process, and preparing for it thoroughly can be the difference between a good application and a successful one. The interview is not simply a formality; it is where the selection committee evaluates your communication skills, motivation, and the depth of your commitment to your proposed study or research in Germany.

Common questions focus on three areas: your academic background, your reasons for choosing Germany, and your future plans after completing your studies. You should expect to explain your research interests in clear, non-specialist language and to demonstrate that you have thought carefully about how your proposed programme fits into your broader career goals.

Preparation starts with reviewing your own application thoroughly. The interviewers will have read your study plan, CV, and recommendation letters, and they may ask you to expand on specific points. Know every document you submitted and be ready to discuss any detail in depth.

Practise answering questions about why you chose your specific German university and programme. Generic responses about Germany being a great country will not impress. Instead, reference specific faculty members whose work aligns with yours, particular courses or modules that address gaps in your current knowledge, or research groups whose output you have followed closely.

For Pakistani applicants, be prepared to discuss how your studies will contribute to Pakistan's development when you return. DAAD values the commitment that scholars will apply their knowledge at home, so having a clear, specific vision of your post-graduation plans strengthens your case significantly.

Conduct mock interviews with mentors, professors, or peers who can give you honest feedback. Time your responses so that they are detailed but concise, typically two to three minutes per answer. Speak calmly, make eye contact, and show genuine enthusiasm for your field. The interview is your opportunity to bring your written application to life as a person, not just a set of documents.

DAAD alumni network and long-term professional benefits

One of the most valuable but often overlooked aspects of winning a DAAD scholarship is the lifelong access it gives you to the DAAD alumni network. This global community of former scholars is a professional resource that continues to benefit you long after you return from Germany.

The DAAD alumni network spans more than 200 countries and includes hundreds of thousands of former scholars and researchers. In Pakistan, the DAAD alumni community is active and well-connected, with regular events, seminars, and professional gatherings that keep former scholars in contact with each other and with ongoing academic developments in Germany.

For your career, this network opens doors in several practical ways. Alumni who have returned to positions in Pakistani universities, government agencies, and private companies often become mentors or collaborators for newer scholars. The shared experience of studying in Germany creates a natural bond that makes professionals approachable and willing to help.

DAAD also maintains institutional relationships with German and Pakistani organisations that facilitate research partnerships, joint projects, and exchange opportunities. As an alumnus, you are better positioned to access these collaborative frameworks, which can lead to research funding, visiting positions, and joint publications.

The alumni network is also valuable for staying current with developments in German academia and funding. DAAD periodically offers returnee grants, short-term research visits, and professional development opportunities exclusively for alumni. These programmes allow you to maintain your connection to German institutions and update your skills without committing to a full new programme.

From a practical standpoint, listing your DAAD scholarship on your CV signals international competence, academic excellence, and the ability to perform in a competitive environment. Employers and academic institutions in Pakistan recognise the DAAD brand, and it can distinguish you in job applications, promotion considerations, and funding proposals throughout your career.

How to write a convincing DAAD study and research proposal

The study or research proposal is often the most heavily weighted component of a DAAD scholarship application, and writing a convincing one requires a balance between academic rigour and practical clarity. This document must convince the selection committee that your proposed work is original, well-planned, and genuinely feasible within the timeframe and resources available.

Start with a clear statement of your research question or study objectives. Avoid broad topic descriptions and instead articulate precisely what you intend to investigate, develop, or achieve. A well-defined question demonstrates that you have moved beyond general interest to serious academic planning.

Literature review is essential. Demonstrate that you understand the current state of research in your area and can identify specific gaps or unresolved questions. Reference key publications and explain how your work builds upon, challenges, or extends them. This positions your proposal within the existing body of knowledge and shows the committee that your work will make a genuine contribution.

Outline your methodology with enough detail to be convincing but without becoming a textbook. Explain what methods you will use, why they are appropriate for your question, and what data or sources you will work with. If your research involves fieldwork, surveys, laboratory experiments, or archival work, describe the practical logistics that show you have thought through how the research will actually be conducted.

Connect your proposal to your choice of German university and supervisor. Explain why this particular institution offers the best environment for your work, referencing specific resources, research groups, libraries, or laboratory facilities that are essential to your project. This shows the committee that you have done your homework and are not simply sending a generic proposal to multiple institutions.

Finally, explain the significance of your work. Who benefits from the findings? How does your research address a practical need in Pakistan or the broader region? DAAD values research with real-world relevance, so articulating the potential impact of your work strengthens your proposal considerably.

DAAD scholarship for Pakistani students: country-specific guidance

Pakistani students have a well-established pathway to DAAD funding, and understanding the country-specific details of the application process helps you navigate it efficiently. DAAD maintains dedicated programming for Pakistan, and the selection criteria and procedures have some characteristics that differ from the general international process.

First, check which DAAD programmes are currently open to Pakistani nationals. Not every DAAD scholarship scheme accepts applicants from every country, so the starting point is confirming that your chosen programme includes Pakistan in its eligible countries list. The DAAD website and the DAAD information point in Pakistan provide up-to-date guidance on which schemes are accepting Pakistani applications in each cycle.

Application submission for Pakistani applicants typically goes through the DAAD portal and may also require submission of physical documents to the DAAD information point or the German Embassy in Islamabad. Follow the instructions precisely regarding which documents need to be uploaded digitally and which must be submitted as certified hard copies.

Academic credentials from Pakistani universities are generally recognised by DAAD, but you should ensure that your transcripts and degree certificates are properly attested. If your university uses a grading system that differs from the German scale, include a brief explanation or conversion guide with your application to help evaluators understand your marks accurately.

Language proficiency requirements vary by programme. For English-taught programmes, IELTS or TOEFL scores are typically required. For German-taught programmes, you will need TestDaF or equivalent proof of German language ability. Some DAAD schemes also offer the possibility of beginning with a language course in Germany before starting your degree.

The DAAD information point in Pakistan is an underutilised resource. Staff there can answer specific questions about eligibility, document requirements, and application procedures that may not be clear from the website alone. Contacting them early in your preparation process can save you significant time and prevent misunderstandings.

Language requirements beyond the DAAD minimum

Meeting the minimum language requirements for a DAAD scholarship is necessary for your application to be considered, but going beyond those minimums can significantly strengthen your candidacy and your experience in Germany. Invest in language preparation not just as an application checkbox but as a genuine investment in your academic and social success.

For English-taught programmes, the typical DAAD requirement is an IELTS score of 6.0 or higher, or equivalent TOEFL results. However, many competitive programmes at top German universities expect higher scores, and applicants with IELTS 7.0 or above are noticeably more competitive. Strong English also makes it easier to engage with the international academic community, write publications, and present at conferences.

For German-taught programmes, the requirements are more demanding. TestDaF level 4 across all sections or the DSH-2 certificate are commonly required minimums. Achieving these levels requires dedicated study over many months, so begin your German language training well in advance of your planned application date.

Beyond formal requirements, everyday German proficiency makes an enormous difference to your quality of life in Germany. While many academics speak English, daily life from grocery shopping to navigating bureaucracy to building friendships with German colleagues requires at least basic German. Scholars who invest in reaching conversational fluency before or shortly after arriving report significantly better integration.

DAAD itself supports language learning through preparatory courses and language grants. The DKF, or Deutschkurse, programmes offer intensive German courses in Germany, sometimes funded as part of your scholarship package. Taking advantage of these opportunities demonstrates commitment and gives you a head start on cultural integration.

Consider language learning an ongoing process rather than a one-time test. Even after you arrive in Germany, continuing to improve your German through daily practice, university courses, and social engagement will enrich your experience and strengthen your professional profile for your career after graduation.

DAAD scholarship extension and renewal rules

Understanding the extension and renewal rules for DAAD scholarships before you arrive in Germany helps you plan your programme realistically and avoid administrative complications during your studies. Most DAAD scholarships have defined durations, but provisions exist for extensions under certain circumstances.

The standard duration of a DAAD scholarship is tied to the expected length of your programme. Research scholarships for doctoral candidates typically run for three to four months for short research visits or up to four years for full doctoral programmes. Study scholarships for master's students generally cover the standard duration of the degree programme, which is typically two years.

Extensions may be granted if you can demonstrate that you need additional time to complete your programme for legitimate academic reasons. Common justifications include delays caused by fieldwork, data collection challenges, or health issues. The key is to apply for an extension before your current funding period expires rather than waiting until the last moment.

To request an extension, you typically need to provide a written explanation of why additional time is necessary, a supporting letter from your supervisor confirming the need, and evidence of satisfactory academic progress. DAAD reviews extension requests on a case-by-case basis, and approval is not guaranteed, so maintaining strong academic performance throughout your scholarship is important.

Some DAAD scholarships allow renewal for a higher degree level. For instance, if you complete a master's degree on a DAAD scholarship, you may be eligible to apply for a separate doctoral funding award. However, this is a new application, not an automatic continuation, and you must meet the eligibility criteria for the doctoral programme independently.

Financial planning around these rules is essential. Do not assume that your funding will be extended without applying, and do not make commitments that depend on continued funding without first confirming your status. Prudent financial planning, including maintaining some savings as a buffer, protects you against unexpected administrative delays or funding gaps.

Comparing DAAD with Erasmus Mundus and other European funding

When planning to study in Germany, the DAAD scholarship is not the only funding avenue worth considering. Comparing it with alternatives like Erasmus Mundus and other European scholarship programmes helps you identify the best fit for your specific academic profile and career goals.

The Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters and Doctorates are EU-funded programmes that allow you to study at multiple universities across Europe. Unlike DAAD, which is focused specifically on Germany, Erasmus Mundus takes you through a multi-country study experience, typically two or three European institutions. The monthly stipend for Erasmus Mundus is generally higher than for DAAD, at around 1,400 euros per month for master's students, and the programme covers tuition, travel, and insurance.

The fundamental difference is focus. DAAD scholarships are ideal if your primary interest is German academia and you have identified a specific German university or research group that is the best fit for your work. Erasmus Mundus is better suited if you want a broader European exposure and your field benefits from the perspectives of multiple academic traditions.

Country-specific European scholarships offer another alternative. The Swiss Excellence Scholarship, the Dutch Holland Scholarship, the Swedish Institute scholarships, and the French Eiffel Excellence Scholarship all provide fully funded doctoral and postdoctoral opportunities. Each has its own eligibility criteria, and Pakistani students are eligible for several of these programmes.

Funding amounts and conditions vary considerably across these programmes. DAAD typically offers monthly stipends in the range that covers basic living costs in Germany, with additional allowances for health insurance and travel. Erasmus Mundus generally provides a slightly higher stipend but may not always cover the full cost of living in expensive cities like Zurich or Stockholm.

A practical strategy is to apply for DAAD as your primary option while simultaneously submitting applications for Erasmus Mundus and one or two country-specific programmes. This diversified approach increases your chances of securing funding and gives you the flexibility to choose the programme that best aligns with your academic and personal priorities.

Practical region and cost considerations for choosing your German university

Choosing which German university to target for your DAAD scholarship application is one of the most significant decisions in the process, and practical factors such as the city, regional cost of living, and support infrastructure deserve as much weight as the university's ranking. The right choice for your budget and temperament often outperforms the most famous name.

Living costs vary sharply across Germany despite DAAD stipends being broadly consistent. Munich is the most expensive university city, with room rents commonly ranging from 600 to 900 euros per month, followed closely by Frankfurt, Stuttgart, and Hamburg. By contrast, Leipzig, Dresden, Jena, and many cities in the former east of Germany offer student housing for roughly 300 to 500 euros, meaning your DAAD scholarship stretches noticeably further.

Student support for international students is not uniform. Universities with long-established international offices, such as Bonn, Gießen, and Siegen in addition to the large research universities, have sophisticated infrastructure for scholarship holders, including dedicated counselling, German language integration, and social programmes. Look beyond rankings and investigate what each institution actually offers its DAAD-funded students.

Industry connections and research infrastructure matter for your long-term goals. If you plan to move into engineering or applied sciences, cities like Karlsruhe, Aachen, and Erlangen provide direct access to major companies and applied research institutes. If you plan academic careers, examine the department's publication strength and whether any research groups align with your field rather than chasing city fame.

Language immersion is easier in cities with a lower proportion of English speakers. While Berlin is comfortable for international students, smaller cities force more daily interaction in German, which accelerates your language acquisition during the DAAD language year and strengthens your integration. Scholars who study in smaller cities often report faster progression in German proficiency.

A useful practical step is to build a shortlist of three to five German universities and compare them on the cost of student rooms, the availability of English-taught modules in your field, the strength of the international student office, and the research profile of relevant departments. Contact the international office of each shortlisted university directly with questions about DAAD scholarship procedures; their responses reveal how well-organised their support actually is.

Official sources and references

  • scholars4dev.com — official information and resources.
  • topuniversities.com — official information and resources.
  • timeshighereducation.com — official information and resources.

faq.q: Is a DAAD scholarship fully funded?
faq.a: Many DAAD scholarships are fully funded, providing a monthly stipend plus insurance and often a travel allowance. Because German public universities charge little or no tuition, a DAAD stipend frequently makes studies essentially cost-neutral, though benefits vary by programme.

faq.q: What is the DAAD EPOS programme?
faq.a: EPOS (Development-Related Postgraduate Courses) funds master's and some PhD study for professionals from developing and emerging countries in fields relevant to sustainable development. It usually requires a few years of relevant work experience.

faq.q: Do I need to speak German for a DAAD scholarship?
faq.a: Not always. Many programmes are taught in English and require an English test such as TOEFL or IELTS. German-taught courses require proof of German proficiency. Always check the language requirements for your chosen programme.

faq.q: How do I find the right DAAD scholarship?
faq.a: Use the official DAAD scholarship database and filter by your country, degree level, and subject. DAAD is an umbrella for hundreds of programmes, so matching your profile to the correct one is essential.

faq.q: When are DAAD deadlines?
faq.a: Deadlines are programme-specific and often fall many months, sometimes a year, before study begins. Check each programme page early and prepare the detailed documents DAAD requires well in advance.

posts.title: Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters: How to Apply (2026)
posts.metaDescription: How to apply for an Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters in 2026: the €1,400/month EU scholarship, eligibility, deadlines and a winning application strategy.
posts.excerpt: A 2026 step-by-step guide to Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters applications, including the €1,400 monthly scholarship, deadlines and insider tips.
posts.bodyHtml:
Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters are among the most attractive fully funded study opportunities in Europe, and applying for the 2026–27 intake is one of the smartest moves a prospective master's student can make. Funded by the European Union, an Erasmus Mundus program lets you complete a single master's degree while studying in at least two different countries, taught by a consortium of top universities, and with a scholarship of up to €1,400 per month for the full program. For students who want an international, multi-country experience with strong funding, few options compare.

This 2026 step-by-step guide explains how the Erasmus Mundus scholarship works, who can apply, when to apply, and how to build an application that gets shortlisted. The program structure can look confusing at first, so we will break it down clearly.

Key takeaways

  • An Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters (EMJM) is an integrated master's delivered by a consortium of universities in at least two countries, with mandatory mobility between them.
  • The EU scholarship is currently €1,400 per month, up to a maximum of 24 months (€33,600 total), and scholarship holders cannot be charged tuition or mandatory participation fees.
  • For the 2026–27 cycle, most consortia open applications between October 2026 and January 2027 for a September 2027 start.
  • You apply directly to each program's consortium website, not a central portal, and each has its own deadline and limit on how many programs you can apply to.
  • Applicants from anywhere in the world are eligible, and there are a limited number of scholarships per program.

What are Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters?

An Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters is a prestigious, integrated study program jointly designed and delivered by a group of universities, called a consortium, based in different countries. When you graduate, you receive either a joint degree or multiple degrees recognised by all participating institutions. The defining feature is mobility: you spend time studying at two or more universities in different countries, following one common curriculum.

The 2026 Erasmus Mundus scholarship

Under current EU funding rules, the scholarship is a monthly allowance of €1,400 for the official duration of the program, normally up to 24 months, giving a maximum of €33,600. That is a contribution to living, travel, visa and installation costs, and it comes on top of a full waiver of tuition and mandatory participation costs, which programs are forbidden to charge scholarship holders. Some consortia offer an optional separate travel-and-installation payment that reduces the monthly stipend instead, so read each program's exact funding terms.

Eligibility

Anyone from anywhere in the world can apply. You normally need a recognised bachelor's degree, a strong academic record, and the English level each program sets (usually IELTS 6.5–7.0 or equivalent). There are usually limits on how many scholars come from the same country to keep the allocation fair, so applicants from countries with many applicants face stiffer competition for a fixed number of places.

How to apply, step by step

  1. Browse the official European Commission EMJM catalogue to find programs that match your background and goals.
  2. Check each consortium's website for the exact deadline, required documents and application limit, since windows typically run October to January.
  3. Prepare your transcripts, CV, two or three recommendation letters and your English test score early.
  4. Write a tailored motivation letter or statement of purpose that explains why this specific consortium, not a generic master's.
  5. Submit through the consortium portal before its deadline, and keep your confirmation email.

Because you can typically apply to only a limited number of Erasmus Mundus programs per intake, shortlist programs that genuinely fit you rather than applying widely. Our statement of purpose guide and our recommendation letters guide cover the two documents that decide most files.

What happens after you apply

Consortia review files, shortlist, interview some candidates and announce results in the spring. Selected students receive a scholarship agreement with the funding terms, then handle visas and travel, with the first monthly allowance covering many of the setup costs. For the bigger picture on studying in Europe, see our study in Europe for free guide and the full scholarship list.

Erasmus Mundus Tuition and Stipend: What You Actually Receive

The financial package of an Erasmus Mundus Joint Master is one of the strongest in international education, but the exact amount depends on several factors. The EU typically funds scholarship holders with a contribution to participation costs that covers tuition, a monthly living allowance, a travel contribution and an installation cost. At the time of writing, the standard monthly stipend is around 1,400 euros for non-EU students and around 700 euros for programme country students, though these figures can shift with each funding cycle. Tuition fees vary by consortium: some charge nothing to scholarship holders, while others deduct the participation cost contribution directly from the stipend. You must read the individual programme description carefully to understand the net amount you will actually receive each month.

Beyond the basic stipend, the travel allowance is calculated based on the distance between your home country and the first programme country, using an EU distance band table. A student flying from Pakistan to Portugal, for example, would receive a higher travel grant than someone travelling from Germany to Spain. The installation allowance is a one-time payment intended to cover initial costs such as housing deposits, residence permits and basic supplies. Health insurance is usually arranged by the consortium and included in the participation cost, but you should confirm this, as some programmes require you to arrange your own cover. When you add up tuition, stipend, travel and installation, a full Erasmus Mundus scholarship for a non-EU student can be worth more than 50,000 euros over the full duration of the programme.

It is important to understand what the scholarship does not cover. The stipend must pay for rent, food, transport, books and personal expenses, and in cities like Paris, Amsterdam or Stockholm, 1,400 euros a month goes further in some fields than others. Students who choose programmes with expensive host cities should budget carefully and look for ways to reduce accommodation costs, such as university residences or shared flats. Some consortia offer additional top-up grants for students from specific regions or for particular subject areas, so always check the programme page for supplementary funding. Finally, the scholarship is paid in instalments, usually monthly or quarterly, and delays at the start of the programme are common, so arriving with a small emergency fund of at least one month expenses is wise.

The prestige of the Erasmus Mundus label carries value beyond the money. Employers and PhD admissions panels across Europe and internationally recognise the programme as evidence that you were selected through a rigorous, multi-university process. The joint degree or multiple degrees you earn are fully accredited in the countries where the consortium operates, and in most cases they are also recognised by relevant professional bodies. When you complete the programme, you should obtain official documentation of the joint degree from the coordinating university and confirm how it is classified in your home country, particularly if you plan to pursue further study or professional registration in Pakistan.

How to Apply to Multiple Erasmus Mundus Programmes Strategically

One of the most practical advantages of the Erasmus Mundus system is that you can apply to up to three different Joint Master programmes in a single application cycle, all through the same online portal. This policy exists because consortium deadlines and requirements are coordinated by the European Education and Culture Executive Agency, and it gives you a realistic chance of securing a place even if your first-choice programme is extremely competitive. However, applying to three programmes requires a disciplined strategy. You cannot simply copy and paste the same motivation letter: each programme has a distinct curriculum, faculty expertise and set of partner universities, and committees can immediately tell when a letter has not been tailored to their specific offering.

Start by researching programmes on the official Erasmus Mundus catalogue, which lists every funded programme with full descriptions, partner universities, entry requirements and contact details. Pay close attention to the programme structure: how many countries will you study in, what is the core curriculum, what elective tracks are available and what are the thesis and internship arrangements. Look at the academic profiles of the teaching staff and identify whose research aligns with your interests. Check the career outcomes of recent graduates, which some consortia publish on their websites or social media. Once you have shortlisted your three programmes, create a comparison table that maps your background against the stated requirements for each one, and identify the two or three strengths you will emphasise differently in each application.

The motivation letter is where most of your differentiation happens. For each programme, open with a clear statement of why that specific programme attracts you, referencing particular modules, faculty members or the multi-country structure. Then explain how your academic and professional background prepares you for the programme, using specific examples rather than general claims. The third paragraph should address your career goals after the programme, showing that you have thought about how the degree fits into a longer trajectory. Close by explaining what you will contribute to the cohort, drawing on your experience working in diverse teams or your perspective from a specific professional or cultural background. Each letter should feel like it was written for that programme alone, even though the underlying narrative about your goals may be similar across all three.

Letters of recommendation are another area where advance planning saves you from last-minute problems. Most programmes require two academic or professional references, and your referees will need to submit their letters directly through the portal before the deadline. Contact your referees at least six weeks before the deadline, provide them with your CV, your motivation letter draft and a summary of each programme you are applying to, and ask them to write separate letters that address the specific qualities each programme values. Some referees prefer to write one strong generic letter that you can use across applications, but the strongest applications feature referees who have tailored their support to the programme stated selection criteria. Follow up politely two weeks before the deadline to confirm that the letters have been submitted, and again forty-eight hours before closing, as incomplete applications without references are automatically disqualified.

Financial planning also benefits from applying to multiple programmes. While all three may offer similar scholarship amounts, the cost of living varies significantly between host cities, and some programmes include tuition waivers while others deduct participation costs from the stipend. If you receive offers from more than one programme, you will need to compare the net financial package rather than just the headline scholarship figure. A programme in a lower-cost city with a slightly smaller stipend may leave you with more disposable income than a programme in a capital city with a higher award. Additionally, some home-country governments, including Pakistani state schemes, offer supplementary grants for Erasmus Mundus scholars, so check whether your national funding bodies provide top-up support and what the application requirements are.

Erasmus Mundus Language Requirements and Preparation

Language proficiency is a critical eligibility requirement for Erasmus Mundus, and the specific demands vary significantly between programmes. Most English-taught programmes require IELTS scores of at least 6.5 overall with no component below 6.0, or equivalent TOEFL or Cambridge results. Some competitive programmes, particularly those in the social sciences, humanities or public policy, set higher thresholds of 7.0 or above. European-taught programmes may require proof of proficiency in the language of instruction, whether that is French, German, Spanish or another European language, and these requirements can be as demanding as the English requirements for English-taught tracks. Always check the specific requirements on the programme website rather than relying on general Erasmus Mundus guidelines, as each consortium sets its own thresholds.

If your English proficiency is close to but not quite at the required level, you have several options. The most straightforward is to retake the IELTS or TOEFL with focused preparation. Some programmes accept a Duolingo English Test, which can be taken at home and results delivered within forty-eight hours, making it a useful fallback if test centre availability is limited. A small number of programmes will accept a medium-of-instruction letter from your previous university if your degree was taught entirely in English, but this waiver is not guaranteed and should be confirmed directly with the programme coordinator before you rely on it. For Pakistani students who completed their bachelor degree in English-medium institutions, obtaining this letter early is a practical step that can save you from sitting an English test you may not need.

For programmes taught partly or wholly in a European language, preparation should begin well in advance. If you are applying to a programme taught in German, for example, reaching B2 level within a year is realistic with consistent study, but starting from zero requires at least eighteen months. Many Erasmus Mundus programmes include a language preparation module at the start, particularly for programmes where you will study in a country whose language you do not yet speak, but these modules are introductory and will not bring you from zero to academic proficiency. Scholarship committees also view proactive language learning favourably: even if the programme is taught in English, demonstrating that you have begun learning the language of one of the host countries shows commitment to integration and cultural engagement. This is particularly relevant for programmes that include a semester in a non-English-speaking country.

When preparing your application, list all language skills accurately, including any Urdu, regional languages or additional languages you speak. Multilingual ability is an asset in the Erasmus Mundus context, where cohorts are intentionally international and collaborative. In your motivation letter, you can briefly mention your language learning goals as part of your broader preparation for living and studying across multiple European countries. Do not, however, claim proficiency you do not have: interview panels may test your language ability informally, and misrepresenting your level will damage your credibility. If you have taken any language exams beyond IELTS or TOEFL, such as DELF for French or TestDaF for German, include the results in your application, as they provide additional evidence of your readiness for a multilingual programme.

Choosing the Right Erasmus Mundus Consortium for Your Goals

With more than 150 Erasmus Mundus Joint Master programmes available in any given cycle, choosing the right consortium is one of the most important decisions you will make. The programme title alone is not enough: you need to examine the curriculum structure, the partner universities involved, the faculty specialisms, the thesis arrangements and the career outcomes of past graduates. A programme that looks ideal on paper may involve study in cities where the cost of living is prohibitive on the scholarship stipend, or it may be led by a university whose research focus does not align with your interests. Thorough research before you apply saves you from accepting a place that is not the right fit.

Start by reading the programme description on the Erasmus Mundus catalogue in full, not just the headline summary. Pay attention to the study pathway: which university will you attend in which semester, what modules are offered at each location and where will you complete your thesis or final project. Some programmes have a fixed pathway where every student follows the same route, while others offer elective tracks that allow you to specialise. Consider the language of instruction at each location, even if the programme is nominally taught in English, as some modules may be offered in the local language. Look at the partner universities strengths: a programme co-led by a top technical university and a leading social science institution will offer a very different experience from one led by two generalist universities.

Faculty expertise is another critical factor. Browse the programme website for staff profiles and identify whose research interests match yours. If you plan to write a thesis in a specific area, the availability of a supervisor with relevant expertise at one of the partner universities can make or break your experience. Some consortia list recent thesis topics, which gives you a concrete sense of what students actually work on. You can also search for faculty members on academic platforms to read their recent publications and assess whether their work genuinely aligns with your goals. A programme where two or three faculty members work in your area of interest is far more valuable than one with a higher overall ranking but no relevant supervision.

Graduate outcomes provide the most honest assessment of a programme value. Some consortia publish employment statistics, average starting salaries or lists of employers that have hired their graduates. If this information is not available on the website, look for the programme on LinkedIn and see where recent graduates are working. Contact current students or alumni directly: most are happy to answer questions about the academic experience, the quality of supervision, the social life and the practical realities of moving between countries. Ask specifically about the administrative support the consortium provides for visa applications, housing and health insurance at each location, as the quality of this support varies considerably between programmes. A consortium with strong administrative coordination can make the transition between countries seamless, while a poorly organised one can leave you dealing with bureaucracy alone.

Common Erasmus Mundus Application Mistakes and How to Avoid Them

The most frequent Erasmus Mundus application mistake is treating the motivation letter as a personal autobiography rather than a focused argument for why that specific programme is the right next step for you. Committees read thousands of letters that begin with a childhood story or a general statement about wanting to change the world. The strongest letters begin with a clear, specific reason for choosing that programme: a research question you want to pursue, a faculty member whose work inspires you, or a particular combination of study locations that no other programme offers. Keep the opening tight and specific, then expand into your qualifications and goals. Every sentence in the letter should serve the argument that you are a strong candidate for this programme and that this programme is the right match for your trajectory.

A second common error is applying to programmes that do not match your profile. The Erasmus Mundus catalogue includes programmes at every level of specialisation, from highly technical engineering tracks to broad interdisciplinary social science degrees. Applying to a programme whose prerequisites you do not meet wastes one of your three application slots and signals to the committee that you have not read the entry requirements carefully. Before you commit to an application, verify that your bachelor degree is in a compatible field, that you meet the stated language requirements and that any required work experience or prerequisite courses are documented in your application. If you are uncertain whether your background fits, email the programme coordinator before applying: most are responsive and will give you an honest assessment.

Recommendation letters that are too generic or too short are another avoidable problem. A letter that says a student is hardworking and intelligent, without specific examples of academic achievement, research capability or collaborative skills, does not help the committee differentiate you from other applicants. When you ask your referees for letters, provide them with a brief document that includes your motivation letter draft, your CV, the specific programme you are applying to and two or three concrete examples of work or projects you want them to highlight. Ask them to address the programme stated selection criteria directly. A letter that explicitly discusses your ability to work in multicultural teams, for instance, is far more useful for an Erasmus Mundus application than one that focuses solely on your exam results.

Missing deadlines is surprisingly common, partly because the single portal handles applications for all three choices and the deadline applies to all of them simultaneously. Some applicants focus on perfecting one application and run out of time for the others. Create a backwards timeline from the deadline, assigning specific dates for completing each component: motivation letters, language test results, referee submissions and document uploads. The portal can be slow in the final forty-eight hours as thousands of applicants submit at once, so aim to complete your submission at least three days before the official deadline. Check that all documents are uploaded in the correct format and that your referees have submitted their letters before you finalise your application. Once you submit, you will receive a confirmation email: if you do not receive one, contact the programme coordination immediately.

A final mistake that particularly affects Pakistani and South Asian applicants is underestimating the importance of the post-programme plan. Erasmus Mundus is funded as a development and capacity-building tool, and committees want to know how you will use the degree after graduation. Vague statements about wanting to work internationally or pursue further study are not enough. You need to explain specifically what you intend to do in your home country or region, which sector or organisation you aim to contribute to and how the specific skills and networks you gain through the programme will enable you to do that work. The strongest applications present a clear before-and-after narrative: where you are now, what you will gain from the programme and what you will do with it when you return. This is not just a formality; it is one of the selection criteria that committees weigh most heavily.

Erasmus Mundus Funding From Home Country and Supplementary Grants

While the Erasmus Mundus scholarship is the primary source of funding, many students supplement it with grants from their home countries, international organisations and the host universities themselves. Pakistani students should investigate whether the Higher Education Commission of Pakistan offers any top-up grants or travel support for Erasmus Mundus scholars, as bilateral education agreements sometimes include supplementary provisions. Some European university development cooperation offices also offer small grants for students from developing countries, and these are often under-advertised. Checking the programme website, contacting the programme coordinator directly and asking current students about supplementary funding opportunities are all worth the effort before you arrive in Europe.

Host universities sometimes offer additional support that is not included in the Erasmus Mundus scholarship package. This can include access to university residences at subsidised rates, free or discounted language courses, health insurance top-ups and student employment opportunities. Some universities have hardship funds that students can apply for if unexpected expenses arise during the programme, and others offer travel grants for conference attendance or thesis fieldwork. These additional resources are not guaranteed, but they exist at many institutions, and asking about them before you arrive means you can plan your budget more accurately. University international offices are generally responsive to enquiries from incoming Erasmus Mundus students, and a brief email asking about available support can reveal resources that are not listed on the programme website.

Private foundations and international organisations also fund Erasmus Mundus students through supplementary grants. The Open Society Foundations, the Aga Khan Foundation and various European development agencies offer scholarships and grants that can be combined with the Erasmus Mundus award. These grants may cover travel costs, provide additional monthly support or fund specific activities such as language courses or professional development workshops. The key is to research these opportunities early, as most have application deadlines that precede the Erasmus Mundus application deadline. Applying for supplementary grants in parallel with your Erasmus Mundus application is a practical strategy that maximises your funding options without creating additional workload during the most intensive period of your application.

When budgeting for the Erasmus Mundus programme, it is worth creating a detailed spreadsheet that maps your expected income against your expected costs for each semester. Include the scholarship stipend, any supplementary grants, personal savings and expected part-time income on the income side, and tuition, accommodation, food, transport, health insurance, books, travel between study locations and personal expenses on the cost side. This exercise reveals whether your budget is realistic and whether you need to take steps to increase your income or reduce your costs. For students from Pakistan, the cost of living in Western European cities can be a shock, and arriving with a clear budget prevents financial stress that can affect academic performance. The Erasmus Mundus student community is also a practical resource: current and former students share budgeting tips, accommodation recommendations and cost-saving strategies that are specific to each programme and each study location.

Erasmus Mundus Degree Recognition and Professional Registration in Pakistan

The recognition of your Erasmus Mundus degree in Pakistan is an important consideration for your long-term career, particularly if you plan to pursue professional registration or return to the Pakistani academic or professional system. Erasmus Mundus Joint Master degrees are awarded by the consortium and are accredited in the countries where the partner universities are located. In most cases, this means the degree is recognised across the European Union and in countries that have mutual recognition agreements with the EU. For Pakistani graduates, the practical question is whether the degree will be recognised by the relevant Pakistani authorities, including the Higher Education Commission (HEC), professional regulatory bodies and potential employers.

The HEC has a process for recognising foreign degrees, and Erasmus Mundus degrees, which are issued by established European universities, are generally accepted through this process. However, the recognition process requires documentation that you should prepare before you leave for Europe. This typically includes the original degree certificate, a transcript of courses and grades, proof that the university is accredited in its home country and a detailed course description. Having these documents translated into Urdu or English (as required) and notarised before you leave Europe saves you from dealing with European bureaucracy after you have departed. Some Pakistani employers or professional bodies may additionally require verification of your degree through the relevant European education authority, so understanding these requirements early in your programme is practical.

For Pakistani graduates in regulated professions, such as engineering, medicine, architecture and law, the recognition process is more complex. Professional registration in Pakistan is managed by sector-specific bodies, such as the Pakistan Engineering Council, the Pakistan Medical and Dental Council and the Pakistan Council of Architects and Town Planners. These bodies have their own criteria for recognising foreign qualifications, and in some cases, additional assessments or examinations may be required before you can practise in Pakistan with your Erasmus Mundus degree. Contacting the relevant regulatory body before you begin your programme, explaining your qualification pathway and asking about the recognition process ensures that you are not surprised by additional requirements when you return.

The Erasmus Mundus degree itself carries significant weight with Pakistani employers, particularly in the private sector, international organisations and the development sector. The competitive selection process, the multi-country study experience and the European accreditation of the degree are all markers that Pakistani employers recognise and value. In the academic sector, an Erasmus Mundus degree from a well-known consortium can strengthen your candidacy for faculty positions at Pakistani universities, particularly if your research area aligns with the university priorities. For government positions, the recognition process is typically straightforward, but understanding the specific documentation requirements of the hiring authority before you apply prevents delays in your employment. The Erasmus Mundus Alumni Association can also provide guidance on degree recognition and career planning, as many alumni have navigated the same process before you.

Preparing Your Documents for the Erasmus Mundus Application

The documentation requirements for Erasmus Mundus applications are specific, and preparing them early prevents last-minute stress. Every consortium requires certified copies of your academic transcripts, your degree certificate, a valid passport, language proficiency test results and a CV in the Europass format or a format specified by the programme. Some programmes also require a research proposal, writing samples or evidence of work experience. All documents that are not in English or the language of instruction must be translated by a certified translator, and some programmes require notarisation or apostille certification. Begin gathering these documents at least three months before the application deadline, as obtaining certified copies and translations from your university or relevant authorities can take several weeks.

The Europass CV format is widely accepted across European institutions and provides a standardised way to present your academic and professional background. If the programme specifies a different format, follow their instructions precisely. Your CV should highlight your education, work experience, research activities, publications, language skills and any awards or recognitions you have received. Keep the CV concise, ideally no more than two to three pages, and focus on the experiences that are most relevant to the programme you are applying to. For Pakistani applicants, including any experience with international organisations, cross-cultural projects or multilingual environments strengthens the CV by demonstrating the qualities that Erasmus Mundus values.

Language test results must be sent directly from the testing agency to the programme or uploaded as certified copies through the application portal. Plan your test date at least two months before the application deadline to allow time for results to be processed and delivered. If your test scores are close to but not quite at the required level, consider retaking the test with targeted preparation rather than relying on borderline scores, as programmes may not make exceptions for applicants who fall slightly below the threshold. Some programmes accept the Duolingo English Test as an alternative to IELTS or TOEFL, which can be taken at home and provides results within forty-eight hours, making it a useful backup option.

When uploading documents to the application portal, verify that each file is in the correct format (usually PDF), is clearly legible and does not exceed the file size limit. Name your files clearly, using a convention such as your surname and the document type, so that the admissions committee can easily identify each file. Before you finalise your application, review every uploaded document to confirm that it is the correct version, that your name appears consistently across all documents and that any translations are complete and accurate. A well-organised, error-free application signals professionalism and attention to detail, and it ensures that the committee evaluates your candidacy on its merits rather than being distracted by administrative shortcomings.

  • erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu — official information and resources.

Erasmus Mundus scholarship components

What the Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters scholarship covers.

ComponentCoveredNotes
TuitionYesPaid to the consortium
Travel costsYesContributions towards international travel
Installation allowanceYesOne-off on arrival
Monthly allowanceYesPaid by the consortium
Language coursesYesShort courses where relevant
