posts.title: IAESTE Internships: Paid Work Abroad for STEM
posts.metaDescription: IAESTE internships give STEM students paid work experience abroad in 80+ countries. Learn how the exchange works, who can apply, and how to get a placement.
posts.excerpt: A guide to IAESTE internships: paid STEM traineeships abroad through a national committee, covering eligibility, funding, the application process and practical tips.
posts.bodyHtml:
IAESTE internships are among the longest-running and most reliable ways for STEM students to earn real work experience abroad. IAESTE, the International Association for the Exchange of Students for Technical Experience, has been arranging paid technical traineeships since 1948, and today its network spans more than 80 member countries. If you are studying engineering, computer science, mathematics or the natural sciences, an IAESTE placement can give you paid work in a company, university or research institute on the other side of the world.

This guide explains what IAESTE actually does, who can apply, how the exchange model works, and how to move through the application process step by step. The single biggest mistake students make with IAESTE is misunderstanding how the system works, so we will make that clear first.

Key takeaways

  • IAESTE arranges paid technical traineeships for STEM students in more than 80 countries.
  • Most placements last 8 to 12 weeks over the summer, though longer internships are available.
  • You apply through your national IAESTE committee, not directly to a central portal.
  • Host employers pay a salary or stipend designed to cover local living costs.
  • The receiving committee helps with housing, insurance and a social programme for interns.

What is IAESTE and how does it work?

IAESTE is a non-profit organisation built on a reciprocal exchange model. A company or university in one member country offers a paid traineeship, and an IAESTE national committee in another country sends a qualified student to fill it. In return, the sending country expects to receive interns for its own employers. This give-and-take keeps the system fair and means that even students from countries with fewer local opportunities can access placements elsewhere.

In practice, you do not apply directly to employers for most positions. Instead, your national committee matches your profile to the offers available to your country and nominates you, which is why contacting your local IAESTE committee early is essential.

Who can apply?

IAESTE internships are aimed at students currently enrolled in a bachelor's, master's or PhD programme, and some committees also accept recent graduates, typically within about a year of finishing. The core focus is STEM: engineering, science, mathematics, information technology and related technical fields. Some positions are open to students from other disciplines, but the vast majority are technical.

You do not need to be a citizen of a member country to apply, but you usually apply through the committee in the country where you study, so check how your institution or country is connected to the network.

Are IAESTE internships really paid?

Yes. IAESTE internships are paid, but the important word is sustainable rather than lucrative. Host employers provide a salary or stipend calculated to cover the local cost of living, so the exact amount varies enormously by country and position. A placement in Switzerland will pay far more in absolute terms than one in Brazil, but both are normally enough for a student to live on during the internship.

Housing is typically arranged or subsidised by the receiving committee, and many committees organise welcome activities, trips and a social programme so interns from different countries meet each other. That combination, a living wage, accommodation support and a built-in community, is what makes an IAESTE summer genuinely affordable.

How to apply step by step

The process is slightly different in every country, but it follows the same broad pattern.

Step 1: Find and register

Search open internship offers on the IAESTE website and register on the exchange platform. Once registered, your national committee can see your profile and match you to offers.

Step 2: Contact your national committee

Your committee guides you through the application, tells you which offers are available to your country, and helps you prepare the required documents, typically a cover letter, CV, transcripts and sometimes language certificates.

Step 3: Get nominated and accepted

If the committee selects you for an offer, your documents are forwarded to the employer, who makes the final decision. Once accepted, you receive details about your start date, insurance and accommodation, and the committee helps with visa paperwork where needed.

What documents do you need?

Prepare a strong cover letter and an up-to-date CV that highlights relevant coursework, projects and technical skills. Many committees also ask for academic transcripts and evidence of English proficiency, since English is the working language for most positions even when the host country speaks another language. If you are unsure how to structure a persuasive motivation letter, our guide to writing a winning statement of purpose covers techniques that apply here too.

Visas and insurance

Because you travel as a trainee rather than a student, visa rules differ from country to country. Some placements are short enough to fall under a visitor visa, while longer internships require a specific work or training visa. The receiving IAESTE committee coordinates most of this, but start early and keep copies of every document. For a general overview of what the process involves, see our student visa guide.

Making the most of your placement

An IAESTE internship is as much about the experience as the salary. Interns come away with real technical experience, an international network and a CV that stands out to graduate programmes and employers. Take part in the social programme, keep a record of the projects you work on, and ask your supervisor for feedback and a reference at the end.

How to apply: next steps

Start by finding the IAESTE office for your country on iaeste.org and asking how the local cycle works, because committees often have their own application windows and deadlines. Prepare your documents, register on the platform, and check the open internships regularly so you can signal interest in the offers that fit you best.

Then treat your IAESTE application with the same seriousness as a job interview, because that is effectively what it is. For more funded international work experience ideas, browse our internships hub and our playbook for funded summer research internships abroad.

Which countries offer the most IAESTE placements and what they involve

IAESTE operates in over 80 countries, but the availability of placements varies significantly by destination. Understanding which countries have the strongest IAESTE programmes and what kinds of work are typically offered helps you target your application strategically.

Germany, Austria and Switzerland consistently offer the largest number of IAESTE placements each year. In Germany, placements are spread across universities, research institutes such as the Max Planck and Fraunhofer societies, and industrial companies in engineering, chemistry, physics and computer science. Austrian placements tend to concentrate in technical universities and manufacturing companies, while Swiss placements often involve research groups at ETH Zurich or EPFL and smaller specialised firms.

Canada is another major IAESTE destination, with placements across universities and research centres in provinces such as Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia and Alberta. Canadian placements are popular because they typically offer competitive stipends, English is the working language in most placements and the country's quality of life is high. Asian destinations including Japan, South Korea, China and India have grown significantly in recent years, offering placements in engineering, information technology and manufacturing with exposure to rapidly developing industries.

European countries such as the Czech Republic, Poland, Hungary and Turkey offer placements at lower cost of living, which means your stipend stretches further. These destinations are particularly attractive for students who want international experience without the high expenses of Western Europe or North America. Latin American countries including Brazil, Mexico and Colombia offer placements in engineering and environmental science, though the number of positions is generally smaller.

The type of work depends on the host organisation. University placements typically involve research assistance, literature reviews, data analysis, laboratory work or technical projects. Industrial placements may involve product testing, quality assurance, process improvement, software development or design work. In all cases, the work is meant to be educational and relevant to your field of study. IAESTE does not place students in routine or unskilled positions; the programme exists to provide genuine professional development.

IAESTE operates through a national committee exchange model, which means your application is handled by your home country's IAESTE committee and placements are arranged through international exchanges between national committees. Understanding this structure helps you navigate the process more effectively.

Step one is to contact your national IAESTE committee. If you are studying in Pakistan, the IAESTE Pakistan committee is based at a major engineering university and handles applications from Pakistani students. If you are studying in the United States, IAESTE USA operates through a centralised system at a host university. Each national committee has its own application deadlines, fees and procedures, so check their website or contact them directly for current information.

Step two is to submit your application to your national committee. The application typically requires academic transcripts, a CV, a statement of interest, a language proficiency declaration and sometimes letters of recommendation. Your national committee reviews applications and forwards a batch of candidate profiles to IAESTE International, which then matches candidates with available placements offered by host committees in other countries.

Step three is the matching process. IAESTE International matches your skills, interests and preferences against available placements. You indicate your preferred countries and types of work, but the final match depends on availability and the decisions of host committees. You may receive your placement offer several months after applying, and the specific host organisation may not be confirmed until closer to the placement date.

Step four is acceptance and preparation. Once you receive a placement offer, you accept it and begin preparing for your stay. This includes arranging a visa if required, securing health insurance, booking flights and making practical arrangements with your host organisation. The entire process from application to placement typically takes four to eight months, which is why applying early is essential. Students who apply in the autumn for a summer placement are in a much stronger position than those who apply in the spring.

Health insurance and visa requirements for IAESTE placements abroad

Health insurance and visa arrangements are two of the most important practical aspects of an IAESTE placement, and they vary significantly depending on your nationality and destination country. Getting these wrong can derail an otherwise excellent placement, so attention to detail here is essential.

Most host countries require IAESTE participants to have health insurance that covers the full duration of the placement. Some host committees arrange group insurance policies for all incoming interns, while others require you to arrange your own coverage. Check with your national committee and the host committee early in the process to understand what is required. If you need to arrange your own insurance, ensure it meets the minimum requirements specified by the host country, which typically include coverage for medical treatment, hospitalisation and repatriation. Budget roughly 50 to 150 US dollars for adequate short-term coverage, depending on the destination and duration.

Visa requirements depend entirely on your nationality and the country where you will be placed. Some countries require a specific intern or trainee visa, while others allow entry on a student visa or a short-term work permit. European countries within the Schengen area may require a long-stay visa for placements exceeding 90 days. Canada typically requires a work permit for IAESTE placements, and the process can take several weeks, so apply well in advance. Japan and South Korea have specific intern visa categories that require documentation from the host organisation.

Your national IAESTE committee will provide guidance on visa requirements for your specific destination, but the ultimate responsibility for obtaining the correct visa rests with you. Start the visa process as soon as you receive your placement confirmation. Gather all required documents, including your placement letter, proof of insurance, financial evidence and any forms required by the host country's embassy or consulate. Processing times vary from a few days to several weeks depending on the country and the time of year.

A common mistake is assuming that a tourist visa is sufficient for an IAESTE placement. In most countries, working on a tourist visa is illegal and can result in deportation and future visa restrictions. Always obtain the correct visa category for your placement, even if the process is more complex. The IAESTE network is experienced in navigating these requirements and will support you, but you need to be proactive and responsive throughout the process. Keep copies of all visa and insurance documents with you during the placement, both physically and digitally.

Making the most of your IAESTE placement for long-term career benefit

An IAESTE placement is more than a summer job abroad. It is a career development opportunity that, if approached strategically, can significantly strengthen your professional profile. The students who benefit most from IAESTE are those who treat the placement as a learning experience rather than simply a way to spend a summer overseas.

From the first day, treat your placement like a professional engagement. Arrive on time, take initiative, ask questions and show genuine interest in the work and the organisation. Supervisors remember interns who contribute actively and are willing to take on challenging tasks. A strong performance can lead to a reference letter, a return offer or a recommendation to a graduate programme, all of which are valuable for your career.

Document your work throughout the placement. Keep a record of the projects you contributed to, the skills you developed and any outcomes or results that followed from your work. This documentation will be useful when you write your CV, apply for graduate school or interview for jobs. Be specific about what you did and what you learned rather than describing the placement in general terms. Quantifiable results, such as the number of experiments conducted, the efficiency improvement achieved or the code modules developed, make your CV entries more compelling.

Build relationships with colleagues and fellow interns. The IAESTE network is global, and many placements bring together students from a dozen or more countries. These connections can become professional contacts, collaborators or friends for life. Attend social events, explore the local area with fellow interns and engage with the workplace community beyond your immediate project. The professional network you build during an IAESTE placement can open doors to future opportunities across multiple countries and industries.

After the placement, follow up with your supervisor and colleagues. A brief thank-you email reinforces the relationship and keeps the door open for future opportunities. Add the experience to your LinkedIn profile and professional CV, including the host organisation, your role and the skills you developed. Mention the placement in future job or graduate school applications as evidence of international experience, technical skills and adaptability. The IAESTE brand is well recognised in academic and industrial circles, and the placement carries weight in selection processes worldwide.

Common mistakes in IAESTE applications and how to avoid them

IAESTE applications are straightforward, but several common errors reduce candidates' chances of receiving a placement. Understanding these pitfalls before you apply helps you present a stronger candidacy.

The first mistake is applying too late. IAESTE placements are filled on a rolling basis through international exchange, and popular destinations and placement types fill early. Students who submit their applications in the spring for a summer placement often find that their preferred destinations are no longer available. Apply as early as your national committee allows, ideally six to eight months before the intended placement start date.

The second mistake is a vague or generic application. When your national committee forwards your profile to IAESTE International, it competes against profiles from students in dozens of other countries. A generic statement of interest that could apply to any placement in any field does not distinguish you. Write specifically about what kind of work you want to do, why you want to do it in a particular country or type of organisation, and how the placement fits your academic and career goals.

The third mistake is ignoring the language and skills requirements. Many placements require English, but some also require or prefer German, French or the local language. If you have language skills, list them prominently and be honest about your level. Similarly, highlight any specific technical skills such as programming languages, laboratory techniques or software tools that are relevant to your field.

The fourth mistake is incomplete or inaccurate documentation. Missing transcripts, unsigned forms, blurred documents or incorrect personal details can delay your application or result in rejection. Review every document carefully before submission. Ensure that your CV is up to date, your transcripts are current and all forms are completed fully and signed where required.

The fifth mistake is unrealistic expectations about the stipend. IAESTE placements provide a stipend intended to cover basic living costs, not a salary. The amount varies by country and host organisation, and in some destinations it may not fully cover accommodation and food. Research the cost of living in your target destination and plan your budget accordingly. Some students supplement their stipend with personal savings, which is perfectly normal and advisable. A well-planned budget ensures you can focus on the work experience rather than financial stress.

Are IAESTE internships really paid and what does the stipend cover

The question of whether IAESTE internships are truly paid is one of the most common concerns for prospective applicants, and the answer requires some nuance. IAESTE internships do come with a stipend, but the amount and what it actually covers vary significantly by country and host organisation. The stipend is intended to cover basic living costs rather than provide a salary equivalent.

In Germany, the typical IAESTE stipend covers accommodation, either provided directly as housing or as a cash allowance, and a monthly cash payment for food and personal expenses. The combined value is enough to live on modestly but not to save money or fund extensive travel. In Canada, stipends tend to be more generous relative to the cost of living, and some host organisations offer additional benefits such as meal plans or transit passes. In Switzerland, the stipend is higher in absolute terms but the cost of living is also much higher, so the purchasing power is comparable to other destinations.

Some host organisations, particularly industrial companies, pay a cash salary on top of or instead of the IAESTE-standard stipend. This is more common in some countries than others and depends on the individual host. When you receive a placement offer, ask the host organisation or your national IAESTE committee specifically about the financial terms. Do not assume that every IAESTE placement comes with the same stipend.

What the stipend typically does not cover includes international airfare, visa fees, personal travel and entertainment beyond basic cultural activities. Budget for these expenses separately, and bring enough savings to cover your first few weeks before the stipend payments begin. In some countries, stipend payments are made monthly in arrears, which means you will need personal funds to cover initial expenses.

The honest assessment is that IAESTE stipends provide a foundation rather than a fortune. They make an international internship financially feasible for students who might otherwise be unable to afford a placement abroad, but they do not eliminate the need for some personal financial planning. Students who approach the placement with realistic expectations and adequate savings have a much more positive experience than those who arrive underestimating the costs involved.

How the IAESTE placement matching process works

The IAESTE matching process is one of the most distinctive features of the programme. Unlike most internship programmes where you apply to a specific host and the host selects you, IAESTE uses a centralised international matching system where your national committee preferences are matched against available placements by the IAESTE International office.

The process begins when your national committee submits your candidate profile, including your academic background, skills, interests and country preferences, to the international matching team. Host committees in other countries submit their available placements, including the host organisation description, the project requirements and the skills they are seeking. The matching team then pairs candidates with placements based on the alignment of skills, interests and preferences.

The matching is not purely algorithmic. Host committees review matched candidates and decide whether to accept them. This means that even if you are matched with a placement, the host committee has the final say. Flexibility in your country and field preferences significantly improves your chances. Students who are willing to go to less popular destinations or who have skills in high demand tend to receive offers faster.

The timeline from application to placement offer is typically three to six months. You may not know your specific host organisation until several weeks before the placement begins. Trust the process: IAESTE has been refining this matching system for decades, and the vast majority of placements result in positive experiences for both the intern and the host.

If IAESTE internships are not available to you because of your field of study, nationality or enrolment status, several alternative programmes offer similar international work experience. The AIESEC global internship programme places students from all disciplines in international work placements, including paid and volunteer positions in business, education and community development. Many countries also have bilateral exchange agreements that include non-STEM fields, so check with your university international office for options relevant to your discipline.

If you are in a STEM field but your country is not an IAESTE member, look at similar programmes run by national organisations. The National Science Foundation funds international research experiences for US students through its IRES programme. The Royal Society of London offers research placements in the UK for international students. The DAAD RISE programme places students from specific countries in German research laboratories during the summer.

If IAESTE placements in your preferred destination are full, consider applying for placements in other countries where demand is lower. IAESTE has branches in over 80 countries, and the availability of placements varies from year to year. A placement in a country you had not initially considered may offer a richer and more surprising experience than the popular destination you had in mind.

Budgeting for an IAESTE placement: realistic costs and savings tips

Understanding the real costs of an IAESTE placement helps you plan financially and avoid surprises. The main expenses to budget for are international airfare, visa fees, health insurance, accommodation beyond what the stipend covers, food, local transport, personal expenses and initial setup costs.

International airfare is typically your largest single expense. Booking at least three months in advance and being flexible with dates can reduce costs significantly. Some destinations are cheaper to reach than others: flights from South Asia to Germany or Austria, for example, are often more affordable than flights to North America or East Asia. Use flight comparison tools and set price alerts to find the best fares.

Visa fees vary by country and nationality. Research the specific requirements for your destination well in advance, as some visas require in-person appointments at consulates that may be located in a different city from your university. Budget 50 to 200 US dollars for visa fees depending on the destination, and add travel costs for any consulate visits required.

Health insurance is mandatory in most host countries. Some IAESTE host committees arrange group insurance, while others require you to arrange your own. Budget 50 to 150 US dollars for adequate short-term coverage. Accommodation costs vary widely: in Germany, student dormitories cost 300 to 500 euros per month, while private accommodation can cost more. Factor in the deposit, which is typically one or two months of rent.

Daily expenses depend on the destination. University canteen meals in Germany cost 3 to 5 euros, while eating out costs 10 to 20 euros. Public transport in most German cities costs 50 to 80 euros per month with a student discount. Personal expenses, weekend travel and entertainment vary by individual but typically range from 100 to 300 euros per month. Total monthly costs for a placement in Germany typically range from 600 to 1,000 euros, which the stipend partially covers.

Practical savings tips include cooking at home rather than eating out, using student discounts for transport and cultural activities, sharing accommodation with fellow interns, and setting a weekly spending limit. Many IAESTE alumni report that careful budgeting allowed them to save modest amounts during their placement, particularly in lower-cost destinations. The key is to plan before you go and to track your spending during the placement.

How to prepare for your IAESTE placement arrival in a new country

The first few days of an IAESTE placement in a new country can feel overwhelming, but thorough preparation makes the transition smoother. Before you leave, research the practical details of your destination: local transport options, banking requirements, mobile phone providers and the location of your accommodation relative to your workplace. Many IAESTE national committees provide welcome packs or online guides with this information, so check your committee resources carefully.

Arrange your airport transfer in advance. Some IAESTE host committees offer airport pickups, while others provide detailed directions and public transport information. If you are arriving late at night or in an unfamiliar city, consider booking a taxi or shuttle service rather than navigating public transport with luggage for the first time. The small additional cost is worth the peace of mind.

Bring essential documents in both physical and digital form: your passport, visa, placement confirmation letter, insurance documents, university enrolment proof and emergency contact information. Keep a printed copy of your accommodation address and the contact details of your host organisation supervisor. Store digital copies in a secure cloud service so they are accessible from anywhere.

On your first day at the host organisation, arrive early, dress professionally and bring your placement confirmation and identification. Introduce yourself to your supervisor and colleagues, and ask about the daily schedule, workplace norms and any immediate tasks you can begin working on. First impressions matter, and demonstrating enthusiasm and initiative from day one sets a positive tone for the entire placement.

In the first week, establish your daily routine: your commute, your meal times, your work schedule and your evening activities. Set up a local bank account if your placement lasts more than a few weeks, and register with any local authorities that require foreign residents to sign in. Buy a local SIM card or mobile plan so you can communicate easily with colleagues, fellow interns and your contacts at home. The sooner you settle into a routine, the sooner you can focus fully on the work and the cultural experience.

IAESTE alumni consistently report that their placement delivered far more than a line on a CV. The experience of working as a paid professional in a laboratory, company or research institute on the other side of the world builds technical skills, professional confidence and a global network in ways that classroom learning cannot match.

Many alumni describe the technical growth as dramatic. Working alongside experienced professionals on real projects, with real deadlines and real consequences, forces you to apply your academic knowledge in ways you have never done before. The feedback you receive, from supervisors and colleagues, sharpens your understanding of your field and teaches you professional standards that employers value. Alumni often report returning to their universities with significantly stronger practical skills and a clearer sense of the career direction they want to pursue.

The cultural and personal growth is equally valuable. Living and working in a foreign country independently, navigating a new language, forming friendships across cultures and adapting to a different workplace environment builds resilience, adaptability and confidence. These qualities are prized by graduate programmes and employers, and they are the kind of development that stays with you for life.

For students considering graduate school, an IAESTE placement provides concrete material for statements and interviews. The ability to describe a specific technical project completed abroad, the challenges faced and the skills mastered, is far more compelling than generic claims about passion for your field. Many alumni received strong reference letters from their IAESTE supervisors, which played a significant role in their graduate admissions success.

Professionally, the IAESTE network is a lasting asset. The connections you build with colleagues, fellow interns and the national committee community can lead to job offers, research collaborations and mentorship opportunities for years after the placement. The IAESTE brand is recognised in academic and industrial circles worldwide, and alumni often find that the placement opens doors that would otherwise remain closed.

posts.title: UN Internships 2026: How to Get a Paid Internship
posts.metaDescription: Which UN internships pay in 2026, who is eligible, stipend ranges by agency, and how to build an application that gets shortlisted.
posts.excerpt: A 2026 guide to paid UN internships at UNICEF, UNDP, UNHCR and beyond, covering stipends, eligibility, where to apply and how to win.
posts.bodyHtml:
UN internships are a common goal for students interested in international development, human rights and global policy, and in 2026 more of them are paid than many people assume. The United Nations runs internships across dozens of agencies and field offices, and several of the best-known bodies, UNICEF, UNDP, UNHCR and WHO, advertise paid roles year-round for students and recent graduates from anywhere in the world. The catch is that the system is decentralised: each agency posts its own vacancies, sets its own eligibility rules and decides its own pay.

This guide cuts through the confusion and explains which UN internships pay in 2026, roughly how much, who is eligible, where to apply, and how to build an application that actually gets read.

Key takeaways

  • UN internships are open to students and recent graduates of all nationalities, with no citizenship requirement.
  • UNICEF pays a monthly stipend of around $1,000 (varies by duty station) plus a one-time travel contribution.
  • UNDP and UNHCR pay stipends to interns who are not otherwise sponsored; WHO and FAO also pay, at varying rates.
  • Parts of the UN Secretariat still advertise unpaid roles, so always read the vacancy before applying.
  • Internships typically last two to six months (UNICEF: six to 26 weeks) and can be in person, hybrid or remote.

Which UN internships pay in 2026?

This is the question everyone asks first, and the honest answer is that it depends on the agency. The big, frequently hiring agencies mostly pay, with stipends set by duty station:

  • UNICEF: around $1,000 per month, plus a one-time lump sum toward travel and visa costs when funding is available. Roles are posted on UNICEF's careers site year-round.
  • UNDP: a monthly stipend set by duty station and work arrangement (including a remote tier), paid to interns who are not already funded by a university or other sponsor. Vacancies appear on jobs.undp.org on a rolling basis.
  • UNHCR: a mandatory stipend for interns without external funding, plus reimbursement of return travel for eligible interns travelling from abroad.
  • WHO and FAO: paid internship schemes with stipends roughly in the $700–1,800 per month range depending on location.
  • Parts of the UN Secretariat: some offices still advertise unpaid internships, so the pay status should be checked on every individual vacancy.

Eligibility

Most UN agencies accept interns who are enrolled in an undergraduate or graduate degree program, or who graduated within the past two years (some agencies accept up to one year). You usually need to be at least eighteen and fluent in at least one working language, most often English. Interns are not UN staff; the arrangement is an experiential learning opportunity, which is exactly why funding policies vary so much across the system.

Where and how to apply

There is no single UN application form. UNICEF posts on unicef.org/careers, UNDP on jobs.undp.org, UNHCR on unhcr.org/careers, WHO on its careers portal, and many bodies also advertise on the central careers.un.org site. Each vacancy has its own deadline, so the practical approach is to check the agency portals regularly and apply to roles that genuinely match your background. Vacancies close when filled, so applying within days of a posting is a real advantage.

Building a strong UN application

UN recruiters read a lot of generic applications, and specificity wins. Tailor your CV and cover letter to the exact duty station, team and mandate of the vacancy, and name the agency's current programmes where relevant. Quantify your experience: instead of "assisted with events", write "coordinated logistics for a fifty-participant workshop". Our guides on writing a winning statement of purpose and building a competitive scholarship profile cover the same skills, and they transfer directly to UN applications.

Practical considerations

Even with a stipend, intern pay rarely covers the full cost of living in cities like Geneva or New York, so plan your budget before you accept an offer. Ask whether the role is in person, hybrid or remote, and clarify visa support early, because agencies vary in how much they can help with paperwork. And be realistic: a UN internship is a strong credential and a networking opportunity, but it does not guarantee a UN job afterwards, so treat it as one step in a longer plan rather than a destination.

How to apply: next steps

Build a clean, tailored CV and a cover letter template now, then start scanning the UNICEF, UNDP, UNHCR and WHO portals. Identify three or four roles that fit your profile, write each application individually, and submit within the first week of each vacancy being posted. If you are not selected, reapply for the next cycle, as many successful UN interns applied several times. For more funded international opportunities, browse our internships hub.

UN Internship Roster Systems and How They Actually Work

Many UN agencies maintain internship rosters that function as talent pools, allowing them to match candidates to positions as they arise rather than advertising each vacancy individually. Understanding how these rosters work is essential for applicants who want to maximise their chances of securing a placement. A roster is essentially a database of pre-screened candidates who have applied and been assessed as potentially suitable for internships within a particular agency or department. When an internship opportunity becomes available, the agency draws from the roster to identify candidates whose skills and qualifications match the position requirements, and these candidates are then contacted directly with an offer or invited to complete a shorter, targeted application process.

The roster approach is used by several major UN agencies, including UNICEF, UNDP, UNHCR, WHO and the World Bank. To get on a roster, you typically need to complete an online profile, submit your academic credentials, work samples and a motivation statement, and pass a preliminary screening. Some agencies conduct interviews for roster inclusion, while others assess candidates based on their written submissions alone. Once on the roster, you remain in the pool for a set period, usually two to three years, during which you may be contacted for internships that match your profile. Being on a roster does not guarantee an internship: it means you are in a shorter queue when a position opens, and the agency may still conduct additional interviews or assessments before making a final selection.

For Pakistani applicants, roster-based internships offer a practical advantage because they allow you to express interest in multiple types of positions within a single agency and to be considered for opportunities across different locations. The UN presence in Pakistan is substantial, with agencies like UNDP, UNICEF, UNHCR, WHO and the FAO all operating field offices, which means that roster candidates in Pakistan may be considered for both headquarters and field-based positions. When completing your roster profile, be specific about the types of roles you are interested in, the skills you bring and the locations you are willing to work in. Generic profiles that do not specify a field or role are less likely to be matched to specific opportunities. If your academic background is in a technical field, such as public health, environmental science or data analysis, highlight these skills prominently, as technical internships are often filled through rosters rather than open advertisements.

The practical challenge with rosters is that they are opaque: you will not typically receive feedback on your application, and you may not hear back for months or even years, if at all. Do not treat a roster application as your only strategy. Apply to advertised vacancies, reach out to UN staff in your network for referrals and attend UN recruitment events. The roster is one tool among many, and it works best when combined with active networking and direct applications. Keep your roster profile updated with new skills, languages, work experience and publications, as agencies may review existing roster candidates before advertising a new position externally. If you have not been contacted from a roster within two years, consider updating your profile or reapplying with stronger documentation.

UN Internship Application Tips for Pakistani and Developing Country Candidates

Pakistani applicants face a specific set of challenges when applying for UN internships, and understanding these challenges allows you to address them proactively in your application. The first is competition: UN internships receive applications from candidates worldwide, and Pakistani applicants are competing against graduates from universities in Europe, North America and other parts of Asia. Your advantage lies in demonstrating knowledge of the context in which the UN operates in Pakistan, including development challenges, humanitarian needs and governance issues. If you have academic or professional experience working on issues that UN agencies address in Pakistan, such as climate adaptation, education access, gender equality or public health, this gives you a concrete foundation that many international applicants lack.

The second challenge is the perception of UN internships as being inaccessible to candidates from developing countries. This perception is partly outdated: many UN agencies now actively seek candidates from developing countries, and several agencies have target quotas for regional representation. The paid internship trend, which has been adopted by UNICEF, UNDP and other agencies, is partly driven by a recognition that unpaid internships exclude candidates who cannot afford to work without pay. When you apply, do not assume that your Pakistani background is a disadvantage: frame it as evidence that you understand the operational context the UN works in, that you have firsthand knowledge of the communities the UN serves and that your perspective as a Pakistani candidate adds diversity to the team.

A third consideration is the language profile that UN agencies value. English is a working language of the UN, and fluency is required for most positions, but additional languages can be a significant advantage. Urdu is a valuable language for UN work in Pakistan, and if you speak Pashto, Sindhi, Punjabi or Balochi, these are assets for field-based positions that involve community engagement. Arabic, French and Spanish are the other major UN working languages, and proficiency in any of these opens doors to positions in regions where these languages are spoken. In your application, list all languages with honest self-assessments of your proficiency level, and if you have formal certifications (such as DALF for French or DELE for Spanish), include them. For Pakistani candidates who have studied or worked in multilingual environments, this is an opportunity to stand out.

The application itself requires careful attention to the UN specific competencies framework. UN agencies assess candidates against core competencies that include communication, planning and organising, teamwork, client orientation and conceptual clarity. When writing your application, structure your examples around these competencies and use the STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result) to describe your experience. Avoid vague claims about being a team player or a good communicator: provide specific examples that demonstrate these qualities in action. For Pakistani applicants, examples drawn from academic projects, community work, NGO internships or government interactions are all valid, as long as they show the competencies the UN values. Proofread your application carefully, as errors in a UN application are noticed and can undermine an otherwise strong candidacy. If possible, have a mentor or colleague review your application before submission.

UN Volunteers Programme as an Alternative Entry Point

The United Nations Volunteers (UNV) programme is one of the most practical entry points into the UN system, and it is particularly well-suited to Pakistani candidates who want to gain UN experience before or instead of an internship. UNV places volunteers in UN agencies worldwide, with assignments ranging from two months to two years, and provides a monthly living allowance, health insurance and a travel grant. The programme is open to candidates aged 25 and older with a bachelor degree and at least two years of professional experience, though younger candidates with relevant skills may also be considered. The monthly stipend varies by location and is intended to cover basic living costs, not to provide a salary in the conventional sense, but for many Pakistani candidates the financial support makes volunteering sustainable in a way that unpaid internships are not.

UNV assignments are available in a wide range of fields, including governance, education, health, environment, human rights and emergency response. Many assignments are based in field offices, which means you could be posted within Pakistan, in a neighbouring country or in another region entirely. Field-based UNV assignments are particularly valuable for Pakistani candidates, as they provide hands-on experience in the operational environments where UN agencies do their most visible work. The application process for UNV involves creating an online profile, indicating your fields of interest and preferred locations and applying to specific assignments as they are posted. Successful candidates are matched to assignments based on their skills, experience and the needs of the UN agency requesting a volunteer.

The advantages of the UNV route over a traditional internship include the financial support, the professional-level responsibility and the duration of the assignment. While internships typically involve supporting staff with tasks, UNV assignments often involve independent responsibility for specific outputs, such as writing reports, coordinating activities or managing small projects. This level of responsibility is more valuable for your professional development and for your CV, as it demonstrates that you can operate effectively within the UN system. Many UNV alumni have gone on to secure regular UN positions, as the volunteer experience provides both the skills and the network needed to compete for professional roles.

For Pakistani candidates considering the UNV route, there are a few practical considerations. The programme requires a commitment to the full duration of the assigned placement, so you should be prepared to relocate if necessary and to commit to the timeline. The application process can be slow, with several months between submission and placement, so patience is important. You will need to provide academic transcripts, references and a motivation statement, and some assignments require additional documents such as a valid passport and medical clearance. The UNV experience is most valuable when it aligns with your longer-term career goals, so choose assignments that build on your existing skills and introduce you to the areas of UN work you want to pursue. Pakistani candidates who have prior experience in development, governance or humanitarian work are particularly competitive for UNV assignments, as the programme values candidates who can contribute immediately.

Building a Strong UN Internship Application: Documents and Strategy

A strong UN internship application is built on three foundations: a compelling motivation letter, a well-structured CV and evidence that you understand the UN work and the specific agency mandate. The motivation letter should be tailored to the specific internship you are applying for, not a generic letter sent to every vacancy. Start by explaining why you are interested in that particular agency and that particular department, referencing recent reports, initiatives or campaigns that the agency has led. Then describe the specific skills and experience you bring, linking them directly to the internship description. Close by explaining what you hope to gain from the experience and how it will contribute to your career goals. Keep the letter to one page, use clear and concise language and avoid repetition.

The UN uses a specific CV format for some applications, and even when a custom format is not required, following the UN conventions helps your application pass initial screening. The UN CV format emphasises education, work experience, languages and skills in that order, with each entry including the title of the position or programme, the organisation, the dates of attendance or employment and a brief description of your responsibilities and achievements. Use action verbs to describe your experience: coordinated, analysed, facilitated, produced, managed. Quantify your achievements wherever possible: the number of people reached, the budget managed, the report produced. For Pakistani applicants, experience with government agencies, NGOs, research institutions and community organisations is all relevant, as long as it demonstrates competencies the UN values.

Supporting documents strengthen your application significantly. Academic transcripts, certificates of completion for relevant training programmes, writing samples and publications all provide evidence of your capabilities. If you have research experience, including a writing sample such as a research paper, policy brief or analysis report allows the hiring panel to assess your analytical and communication skills directly. References are important: choose referees who know your work well and can speak specifically about your skills and achievements. A reference from a UN staff member, if you have one, carries additional weight, but a strong reference from a university professor or professional supervisor is equally valid. Ensure your referees are aware that they may be contacted and that they have agreed to provide a reference for you.

Strategic networking is an often-overlooked element of the UN internship application process. Attending UN events, webinars and conferences, joining UN-related professional groups on LinkedIn and reaching out to current or former interns for advice can provide insights that improve your application. If you can identify and contact a staff member in the department you are applying to, a brief and professional email expressing your interest in the internship and asking for any guidance on the application process can make your application more visible. This approach must be handled with care: be respectful of the person time, do not ask for a favour and keep the email short and focused. For Pakistani candidates, the UN presence in Pakistan means that there are often local events, workshops and networking opportunities that you can attend to build connections with UN staff in your area.

Common Mistakes in UN Internship Applications and Interview Preparation

The most common mistake in UN internship applications is submitting a generic application that does not address the specific role or agency. UN hiring panels review hundreds of applications for each internship, and applications that could have been written for any vacancy are immediately distinguishable from those that demonstrate genuine knowledge of the agency work. Before you apply, read the agency recent strategic plan, annual report or key publications, and reference these in your motivation letter. Explain how your skills align with the specific tasks listed in the internship description, not just the agency general mission. This level of specificity shows the panel that you have invested time in understanding the role and that you are applying thoughtfully rather than casting a wide net.

A second frequent error is failing to demonstrate the UN core competencies in your application. The UN assesses candidates against competencies such as communication, teamwork, planning and organising, professionalism and client orientation. Your application should provide concrete examples of each competency, drawn from your academic, professional or volunteer experience. If the internship description mentions specific competencies, address each one explicitly in your application. For Pakistani applicants, examples from community engagement, academic group projects, NGO work or government internships are all valid, as long as they show the competency in action. Avoid generic claims: instead of saying you are a good communicator, describe a specific situation where your communication skills produced a measurable outcome.

Interview preparation for UN internships follows a different pattern than for private sector positions. UN interviews typically involve behavioural questions that probe your competencies, situational questions that test your judgement and technical questions related to the specific role. Prepare by reviewing the competency framework for the agency you are interviewing with, practising STAR-format answers to common behavioural questions and researching the specific issues the department works on. For Pakistani candidates, be prepared to discuss how your experience relates to the UN work in Pakistan, including development challenges, humanitarian responses and governance issues. The panel may also ask about your ability to work in multicultural teams, your experience with UN systems or tools and your availability for the full internship period.

Post-interview follow-up is a small but important step. After a UN interview, send a brief thank-you email to the panel or the contact person, reiterating your interest in the role and summarising one or two key points from the interview that you want to reinforce. This is not a common practice in all cultures, but it is appreciated in the UN context and can leave a positive impression. If you are not selected, request feedback if possible: some agencies provide feedback to unsuccessful candidates, and the insights you gain can improve future applications. The UN recruitment process is lengthy, and it is common to apply multiple times before securing a position. Treat each application as a learning experience, refine your approach based on the feedback you receive and persist. Many successful UN professionals applied for internships and entry-level positions multiple times before securing their first role, and the persistence and self-improvement they demonstrated along the way are themselves evidence of the competencies the UN values.

Writing a UN Internship Motivation Letter That Stands Out

The motivation letter is the most important document in a UN internship application, and it is where you distinguish yourself from the hundreds of other candidates who meet the basic eligibility requirements. A strong UN motivation letter does three things: it demonstrates genuine knowledge of the agency work, it connects your specific skills and experience to the internship description and it explains how the experience will contribute to your career goals. The letter should be one page maximum, written in clear and concise English, and structured around the specific competencies and responsibilities listed in the internship advertisement. Avoid generic statements about wanting to work for the United Nations or about being passionate about international development: these are sentiments that every applicant expresses, and they do not differentiate you.

Start your letter by explaining why you are interested in that particular agency and that particular department. Reference specific reports, campaigns, initiatives or publications that the agency has produced, and explain how they connect to your academic or professional interests. This demonstrates that you have researched the agency and that your interest is specific rather than generic. Then describe the skills and experience you bring, linking each one directly to a requirement or responsibility listed in the internship description. Use concrete examples: instead of saying you have strong analytical skills, describe a specific analysis you conducted and the outcome it produced. Instead of saying you are a good communicator, describe a specific instance where your communication skills produced a measurable result. The third paragraph should explain how the internship will contribute to your career goals, showing that you have thought about how this experience fits into a longer professional trajectory.

The UN specific competencies should be woven throughout your letter, not listed as a separate section. The core competencies that UN agencies assess include communication, teamwork, planning and organising, professionalism and client orientation. For each competency, provide one or two specific examples from your academic, professional or volunteer experience. If the internship description mentions specific competencies, address each one explicitly. The STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result) provides a useful structure for these examples, ensuring that you provide enough context for the reader to understand the situation, the action you took and the outcome you achieved. For Pakistani applicants, examples from academic research, community engagement, NGO work and government interactions are all valid, as long as they demonstrate the competencies in action.

Proofreading and presentation matter more in a UN application than in many other contexts. The UN receives applications from candidates around the world, and the quality of your English, including grammar, spelling and punctuation, is assessed as part of the evaluation. Errors in a motivation letter suggest carelessness or insufficient English proficiency, both of which can undermine an otherwise strong application. After you have drafted your letter, read it aloud to check for flow and clarity, ask a native English speaker to review it for grammar and idiomatic accuracy and check that it addresses every point listed in the internship description. Submit the letter in the format specified by the agency, usually as a PDF attachment, and ensure that your name and the internship reference number are clearly stated on the document.

UN Internship Work Environment and What to Expect on the Job

Understanding the UN work environment before you begin your internship helps you adapt more quickly and make a stronger impression during your placement. The UN work culture varies between agencies and between headquarters and field offices, but several characteristics are broadly consistent. The UN operates in a multilingual, multicultural environment where English is the primary working language, but you will interact with colleagues who speak many different languages and come from diverse professional backgrounds. Decision-making in the UN is often consensus-based and bureaucratic, which means that processes can be slower than in the private sector, but it also means that every voice is heard and every perspective is considered. Understanding this culture of deliberation, and adapting your working style to it, is an important part of a successful internship.

As an intern, you can expect to be assigned specific tasks and projects that contribute to the work of your team. These tasks may include research, data analysis, report writing, event coordination, translation, database management or communication support, depending on the department and the internship description. The most successful interns are those who take initiative: rather than waiting to be told what to do, they identify needs, propose solutions and volunteer for additional responsibilities. This proactive approach is valued in the UN system and can lead to additional responsibilities, stronger references and potential job offers. At the same time, respect the boundaries of your role: as an intern, you are there to learn and to contribute, not to make decisions or to bypass established processes.

The UN work environment includes a strong emphasis on teamwork and collaboration. You will work with colleagues from different units, departments and even agencies, and the ability to work effectively in a team is one of the core competencies that the UN assesses. Demonstrate your teamwork skills by being responsive to emails, meeting deadlines, sharing information with colleagues and contributing constructively to group discussions. The UN also values a culture of continuous learning: attend training sessions, workshops and seminars that are offered to staff and interns, and use them to build skills that are relevant to your career goals. Many UN offices have internal learning platforms that provide access to online courses, webinars and professional development resources, and taking advantage of these during your internship adds value to your experience beyond the tasks you are assigned.

For Pakistani interns, the UN work environment may feel different from the professional cultures you are accustomed to. The UN places a strong emphasis on gender equality, diversity and inclusion, and these values are reflected in everyday workplace interactions, hiring practices and programme design. Demonstrating awareness of and commitment to these values in your work and your interactions is important. The UN also has strict rules on impartiality, neutrality and conflict of interest, and as an intern you are expected to comply with these rules. Understanding the UN code of conduct, the standards of behaviour and the reporting mechanisms before you begin your internship prevents misunderstandings and ensures that you represent yourself and your country professionally throughout your placement.

UN Internship Platforms and Where to Find Current Openings

Finding current UN internship openings requires knowing where to look, as opportunities are posted across multiple platforms depending on the agency. The UN careers portal (careers.un.org) is the central hub for vacancies across the UN system, and it lists internships alongside regular positions. However, many agencies also post internships on their own dedicated platforms. UNICEF uses its own careers site, as does UNDP, UNHCR and WHO. The World Bank posts internship opportunities through its dedicated internship page, and the IMF uses its own recruitment system. Checking these platforms regularly, setting up job alerts and following the relevant agencies on professional networking sites ensures that you do not miss opportunities.

Social media is an underutilised resource for finding UN internship opportunities. Many UN agencies and departments use Twitter, LinkedIn and Facebook to announce internship openings, particularly for shorter-term or field-based positions that may not be advertised for long. Following the social media accounts of agencies you are interested in, as well as the accounts of specific departments or regional offices, can alert you to opportunities that you might otherwise miss. LinkedIn is particularly useful, as many UN staff members share internship opportunities in their professional networks, and engaging with UN-related content on the platform increases your visibility to UN recruiters.

The timing of your application matters. Many UN internships follow a seasonal recruitment cycle, with summer internships advertised between January and March and winter or spring internships advertised between August and October. However, some agencies recruit on a rolling basis, and field-based internships may be advertised at any time depending on operational needs. Applying early in the recruitment window, rather than waiting until the deadline, gives you an advantage, as many agencies begin reviewing applications as soon as they are received. Setting up a calendar reminder for the recruitment cycles of your target agencies ensures that you apply at the optimal time.

For Pakistani candidates, the UN in Pakistan maintains a local presence that can facilitate your search. The UN country team in Pakistan coordinates across agencies, and some agencies advertise local internship opportunities through their Pakistan offices. Contacting the human resources or admin section of UN agencies in Pakistan, expressing your interest and asking about upcoming internship opportunities can open doors that are not publicly advertised. Attending UN events, workshops and seminars in Pakistan also provides opportunities to meet staff members who can advise you on the application process and alert you to relevant vacancies. Building these local connections, combined with regular monitoring of the global platforms, creates a comprehensive search strategy that maximises your chances of finding and securing a UN internship.
