faq.q: Can I immigrate to Switzerland without a job offer?
faq.a: No for third-country nationals. An employer must apply for your permit through the canton, proving no Swiss or EU/EFTA candidate was available. There is no points-based independent route and no digital-nomad visa.

faq.q: Is there an EU Blue Card in Switzerland?
faq.a: No. Switzerland is not in the EU and has no EU Blue Card. Third-country admission runs through quotas (8,500 permits in 2026) and a case-by-case labour-market test, with no fixed salary threshold.

faq.q: How long does it take to get Swiss permanent residence?
faq.a: The C permit (permanent residence) comes after 10 years for most third-country nationals (5 for EU/EFTA nationals and some US/Canadian nationals). Citizenship needs 10 years of continuous residence plus integration including A2–B1 language.

faq.q: What are the Swiss work permit quotas for 2026?
faq.a: 8,500 permits for third-country nationals (4,500 B residence + 4,000 L short-stay), unchanged from 2025. Separate quotas cover EU/EFTA service providers (3,500) and UK nationals (3,500).

faq.q: Can I switch from a tourist visa to a work permit in Switzerland?
faq.a: No. The Schengen C visa is short-stay and cannot be converted into a work permit. A Swiss employer must apply for your B or L permit via the canton while you are outside the country.

posts.title: How to Immigrate to Italy: Blue Card & Permits
posts.metaDescription: How to immigrate to Italy in 2026: the EU Blue Card (€35,500 salary), Decreto Flussi quotas, work visas and the 5-year path to PR.
posts.excerpt: The two real doors into Italy in 2026: the quota-free EU Blue Card for professionals and the Decreto Flussi lottery for other workers.
posts.bodyHtml:
immigrate to Italy Italy's immigration system has two very different doors. For qualified professionals, the EU Blue Card is fast, quota-free and available year-round, requiring a salary of around €35,500 and a valid job offer. For everyone else, the Decreto Flussi is an annual quota lottery that opens on a "click day" and typically fills within minutes. This guide explains both routes, plus the digital-nomad visa and the study-first path, so you know which door actually fits your profile before you start.

If you are a university-educated professional, or have five years of relevant experience, the Blue Card is almost always the smarter play than waiting for a quota window.

Key takeaways

  • The EU Blue Card is Italy's skilled route: quota-free, year-round, for a highly qualified job paying at least €35,000–35,500 gross a year (reduced to ~€28,200 in shortage sectors like ICT and healthcare).
  • The Decreto Flussi is the annual capped quota (around 150,000 slots in 2025) for seasonal, subordinate and trade work, applied for by employers on the click day.
  • Your employer secures a Nulla Osta (work authorisation) first; you then apply for a Type D work visa and convert it to a residence permit within eight working days of arrival.
  • The study-first route is often the most reliable: convert your student permit to a work permit any time, no quota window needed.
  • Permanent residence comes after 5 years of legal residence; citizenship after 10 (4 for EU citizens).

The EU Blue Card: Italy's skilled route

The Blue Card is for university-educated professionals or those with five years' professional experience equivalent to a higher-education qualification. You need a job offer for a highly qualified position with a contract of at least 12 months and a salary meeting the threshold: €35,000–35,500 gross per year (1.5x the national average), or around €28,200 in shortage sectors such as ICT and healthcare. The salary must be base salary, not bonuses, and must also meet the minimum set by the relevant collective agreement. Processing runs 60–120 days total (Nulla Osta 30–90 days), the permit lasts one to two years and renews up to four years and beyond, and spouses and children join with immediate work rights. After 18 months, Blue Card holders gain EU-wide mobility, and time on the card counts toward long-term residence.

The Decreto Flussi quota route

Each year a decree sets how many non-EU workers may enter Italy for employment, around 150,000 slots in 2025, split between seasonal, non-seasonal subordinate, self-employment and conversions. Employers submit on the "click day", first come, first served, and the window is often exhausted within minutes, which is why most successful applications are filed by an experienced Italian lawyer the moment it opens. Duration is usually two years for subordinate work, and it builds the residence history you need for PR after five years, though seasonal work does not lead to residence directly.

Digital nomad and other routes

The digital-nomad visa, introduced in 2024, suits highly skilled remote workers earning from abroad: roughly €28,000 a year in income, health insurance and accommodation proof, valid one year and renewable. The Italia Startup Visa is quota-free for founders of innovative startups, with a decision in about 90 days. Intra-company transfers and family reunification (spouses, minor children and dependent parents, with work rights) round out the picture. Retirees and people of independent means can use the elective residence visa, which requires passive income of roughly €31,000+ a year and allows no work.

The study-first route

International graduates of Italian universities can convert their student permit to a work permit at any time, with no Flussi window since the 2023 reform, and can take a 12-month job-search permit. Tuition at Italian public universities is low (often €1,000–3,000, and sometimes less), so studying first is both cheaper and strategically smarter than competing for quota places from abroad. See our study in Italy guide for the full picture.

How to Immigrate to Italy: Blue Card & Permits: what this guide covers

This guide explains everything a Pakistani student needs to know about immigrate to Italy, including eligibility, costs, timelines and practical steps. Use the sections above to find the exact information you need, or bookmark this page and return as your application progresses.

Costs, PR and citizenship

Key 2026 fees: Type D work visa about €116, residence permit (permesso di soggiorno) around €70.50, and Schengen tourist visa €90. Permanent residence (Permesso di Soggiorno UE) comes after 5 years of continuous legal residence, and citizenship after 10 years (4 for EU citizens) with B1 Italian and a clean record. Italy permits dual nationality. For the complete breakdown of every route, fee and the official sources, see our immigrate to Italy guide.

How to Immigrate to Italy Through the Study Route

For many Pakistani professionals and graduates, the study-first route is the most practical way to immigrate to Italy, because it sidesteps the quota restrictions that govern work permits. Italy allows international students to apply for a student visa (type D) for enrolment in Italian universities, and upon arrival you can apply for a residence permit that covers the duration of your studies. The key advantage is that as a student, you are not counted against the Decreto Flussi quota, and you have twelve months after graduation to convert your student permit into a work permit if you find employment. This conversion window is one of the most valuable features of Italy immigration system for non-EU nationals, and it gives you time to build professional connections, secure a job offer and navigate the permit conversion process without the pressure of an expiring visa.

To use the study route effectively, you need to secure admission to an Italian university before applying for your visa. Italian universities offer programmes in both Italian and English, and the number of English-taught programmes has grown significantly in recent years. The application timeline varies by university: some use the Universitaly portal for pre-enrolment, while others have their own application systems. Pakistani students should begin researching programmes at least nine months before the intended start date, as the visa application process through the Italian Embassy in Islamabad or the Consulate in Karachi can take several months. You will need to demonstrate financial capacity (at the time of writing, around 6,500 euros per year or equivalent), have valid health insurance and provide proof of accommodation in Italy.

Once in Italy, the conversion from student to work permit requires a job offer from an Italian employer and a valid residence permit that has not expired. The employer must initiate the work permit application, which is submitted to the immigration office (Sportello Unico per l Immigrazione) in the province where you will work. If you hold a degree from an Italian university, you may be exempt from the Decreto Flussi quota for the initial work permit conversion, depending on the specific regulation in force at the time. This exemption does not apply indefinitely, so timing is important: apply for the conversion as soon as you have a qualifying job offer. After five years of legal residence in Italy, you can apply for long-term resident status (soggiorno UE per soggiornanti di lungo periodo), which gives you greater flexibility to work and change employers without needing a new permit.

The study route also offers a useful pathway for those who want to pursue academic careers. Italy university system hires researchers and lecturers on fixed-term contracts, and securing a research position at an Italian university can lead to a work permit that is independent of the Decreto Flussi. If your field is in STEM, medicine, architecture or another area where Italian universities actively recruit international talent, the academic route can be faster and less bureaucratic than the standard employment route. Some Italian universities also participate in the EU Blue Card system, which provides an accelerated path to a work permit for highly qualified employment. Combining a master or doctoral degree at an Italian university with a research position or Blue Card-eligible job creates a realistic long-term immigration strategy that does not depend on winning a quota lottery.

The EU Blue Card in Italy: Requirements and Advantages

The EU Blue Card is Italy most straightforward route to a work permit for qualified professionals, and unlike the Decreto Flussi, it is not subject to annual quotas. The Blue Card is available year-round, and the application can be submitted at any time as long as you have a valid job offer from an Italian employer. To qualify, you need a higher education degree (at least a three-year bachelor or equivalent), a job contract of at least one year and a gross annual salary that meets the threshold set by Italian law. At the time of writing, the minimum salary for a Blue Card in Italy is around 35,500 euros per year, though this figure is adjusted periodically and should be confirmed with the Italian immigration authorities before you apply.

The Blue Card process begins with the employer. Your employer must submit the application to the immigration office (Sportello Unico per l Immigrazione) in the province where you will work, along with your job contract, degree documentation, passport copies and proof that the salary meets the threshold. The immigration office verifies that the position requires the qualifications you hold, that the salary is genuine and that the employer has the capacity to pay. Processing times vary by province but typically range from four to eight weeks. Once approved, you will receive a nulla osta (authorisation), which you then use to apply for a Blue Card visa at the Italian consulate in your country of residence. Upon arrival in Italy, you must apply for a residence permit (permesso di soggiorno) at the local post office within eight days.

The Blue Card offers several advantages over a standard work permit. First, it provides a path to permanent residency after five years of legal residence, compared to ten years for a standard permit. Second, Blue Card holders have greater mobility within the EU: after eighteen months in Italy, you can move to another EU country and convert your Blue Card into a Blue Card in the new country, subject to that country requirements. Third, the Blue Card is tied to your qualifications, not to a single employer, which means you can change jobs more easily than with a standard permit. Fourth, family members (spouse and dependent children) receive residence permits that are linked to yours, and they are entitled to work in Italy without needing a separate work permit. These advantages make the Blue Card the preferred route for professionals who meet the salary and qualification thresholds.

For Pakistani professionals considering the Blue Card route, the main challenges are obtaining the necessary documentation from Pakistan and meeting the salary threshold in a competitive labour market. Degree documentation must be verified by the Italian consulate in Pakistan, which may require translating and legalising your academic transcripts. If your degree is from a Pakistani university, you may need to have it evaluated by CIMEA (the Italian ENIC-NARIC centre) to confirm its equivalence to an Italian qualification. The salary threshold, while lower than in some other EU countries, may be higher than what many Pakistani professionals earn in their first international position, so researching the salary landscape in your field before you apply is important. Networking with Italian professionals in your field, joining relevant LinkedIn groups and contacting Italian companies directly are practical steps that can help you secure a qualifying job offer.

The Decreto Flussi: How Italy Quota System Works in Practice

The Decreto Flussi is Italy annual quota system for non-EU immigration, and understanding how it works in practice is essential for anyone considering the work-permit route. Each year, the Italian government publishes a decree (decreto) that sets the total number of work permits available for non-EU nationals, divided into categories: seasonal work, non-seasonal work, self-employment and family reunification. The total number of permits fluctuates, but at the time of writing it has been in the range of 80,000 to 150,000 across all categories, with the majority allocated to seasonal agricultural and tourism work. Non-seasonal work permits, which are relevant for permanent employment, typically represent a smaller share of the total.

The application process is competitive and fast-moving. Applications must be submitted online through the Ministry of the Interior portal, and the submission window opens on a specific date each year, often referred to as click day. In recent years, the window for non-seasonal work permits has opened in the morning and closed within hours, sometimes within minutes, as applications flood the system. Employers must pre-register their job offers through the immigration portal before the application window opens, and all required documentation must be ready to submit the moment the window opens. For Pakistani applicants, this means working with an Italian employer well in advance, ensuring that the job offer is properly registered and having all your documents translated, legalised and ready for submission.

The Decreto Flussi has significant limitations for professionals from countries like Pakistan. The quota for non-seasonal work permits is oversubscribed, and the competitive nature of the click day process means that many qualified applicants are unable to secure a permit. Seasonal work permits, while more numerous, are typically limited to agriculture and tourism, which are not relevant for most professional applicants. Self-employment permits have their own separate allocation and require a different set of conditions, including a clear business plan and proof of financial resources. The practical reality is that the Decreto Flussi is not a reliable route for most professional immigrants from Pakistan, which is why the Blue Card and study-first routes are generally more promising.

If you do pursue the Decreto Flussi route, the process requires close coordination with your Italian employer. The employer must demonstrate that they have been unable to fill the position with an Italian or EU candidate, that they have a valid and active business and that they are willing to sponsor your permit. The employer also bears certain administrative costs, which can deter some smaller companies from participating. Once submitted, the application enters a queue, and permits are allocated in the order they are received, up to the quota limit. If the quota is exhausted before your application is processed, you must wait until the next year decree. Given this uncertainty, the Decreto Flussi should be treated as a secondary option, with the Blue Card or study-first route serving as your primary strategy. Always consult the current year Decreto Flussi before relying on any of these figures, as the quotas and rules change annually.

Italian Permanent Residency and Citizenship Timelines

The path to permanent residency and eventually citizenship in Italy follows a structured timeline, and understanding these milestones helps you plan your immigration strategy from the outset. Permanent residency (soggiorno UE per soggiornanti di lungo periodo) becomes available after five years of continuous legal residence in Italy, during which you must have been employed, self-employed or otherwise financially independent. You must also demonstrate basic Italian language proficiency (at least A2 level under the CEFR framework), have a clean criminal record and prove that your income meets a minimum threshold. The application is submitted to the local questura (police headquarters) and typically takes several months to process. Once granted, permanent residency is valid for five years and renewable, and it allows you to work and live anywhere in the EU without needing a new permit.

Citizenship is available after ten years of continuous legal residence for non-EU nationals, or after four years if you are married to an Italian citizen. The residency requirement is reduced to three years for those who have been legally resident in Italy for at least five years and have an Italian-born child. The citizenship application is submitted to the local prefecture and processed by the Ministry of the Interior. Processing times are notoriously long: at the time of writing, applications commonly take two to four years to be decided, and the process involves background checks, language assessment and an interview. Italian citizenship grants you full EU citizenship, including the right to live and work anywhere in the EU, vote in Italian elections and hold an Italian passport.

For Pakistani immigrants, the citizenship timeline is one of the longest in Europe, and it requires sustained commitment to life in Italy. The ten-year residency requirement means that you must maintain continuous legal residence, with no extended absences that could break the continuity, and you must meet the income and language requirements for the entire period. Some Pakistani immigrants choose to apply for permanent residency first, which provides most of the practical benefits of citizenship (the right to work, change employers and live in the EU) without the additional bureaucratic burden of the citizenship application. Others pursue citizenship actively, particularly if they have family ties to Italy or plan to remain long-term. The decision depends on your personal circumstances and your long-term plans, but either way, maintaining legal status, paying taxes and demonstrating integration into Italian society are the foundations of a successful application.

A practical consideration that many immigrants overlook is the requirement to renounce your previous citizenship if you acquire Italian citizenship, as Italy does not permit dual citizenship for naturalised citizens (with some exceptions for countries that do not allow renunciation). Pakistani citizens who acquire Italian citizenship would need to renounce their Pakistani citizenship under Pakistani law, which has its own requirements and procedures. This is a significant decision that affects your ties to Pakistan, your property rights, your family obligations and your identity. Many Pakistani immigrants maintain their permanent residency in Italy without pursuing citizenship, which allows them to preserve their Pakistani citizenship while enjoying most of the practical benefits of long-term residence. Discuss this decision with your family and with a legal advisor before committing to the citizenship route.

Practical Challenges and Living Costs for Immigrants in Italy

Italy cost of living varies dramatically between the north and the south, and understanding this variation is essential for financial planning. Northern cities like Milan, Turin and Bologna have higher rents, higher salaries and a more competitive job market, while southern cities and towns offer significantly lower living costs but fewer employment opportunities. At the time of writing, a one-bedroom apartment in central Milan might cost 1,200 to 1,500 euros per month, while a comparable apartment in Naples or Palermo could be 500 to 700 euros. Groceries, transport and utilities follow a similar pattern, with the south being roughly 30 to 40 percent cheaper than the north. For Pakistani immigrants who are establishing themselves, the south offers a more affordable entry point, but the north offers a wider range of professional opportunities, particularly in technology, finance and engineering.

The Italian healthcare system is accessible to legal residents through the Servizio Sanitario Nazionale (SSN), which provides coverage for essential medical services. Once you have a valid residence permit, you can register with the local health authority (ASL) and receive a tessera sanitaria (health card). The system provides good coverage for hospital care, specialist consultations and prescription medication, though waiting times for non-urgent procedures can be long. Many residents also purchase private health insurance to supplement the SSN, particularly for dental care and faster access to specialists. For Pakistani immigrants who are accustomed to different healthcare systems, understanding how to navigate the Italian system, including how to register, how to find English-speaking doctors and how to access emergency care, is an important part of settling in.

The language barrier is one of the most immediate challenges for Pakistani immigrants in Italy. While English is widely spoken in professional and academic settings, everyday life, including interactions with government offices, landlords, banks and healthcare providers, is conducted in Italian. Reaching a functional level of Italian (at least B1) within the first six months of arrival should be a priority. Many cities offer affordable Italian language courses through community organisations, adult education centres (CPIA) or universities. Some professional fields, particularly law, medicine and public administration, require advanced Italian proficiency, so if your career plan involves these sectors, investing in language training from the beginning is essential. Learning Italian also significantly improves your integration into Italian society, your ability to navigate bureaucracy and your long-term prospects for permanent residency and citizenship.

The Italian job market has specific characteristics that affect immigrants. Networking is extremely important: personal connections and professional referrals play a larger role in hiring than in many other European countries, and many positions are filled through informal channels before they are ever publicly advertised. Building a professional network in Italy requires patience and initiative: attend industry events, join professional associations, connect with Italian colleagues on LinkedIn and do not hesitate to reach out to people in your field for informational conversations. The probationary period in Italian employment contracts is typically six months for professional roles, during which either party can terminate the contract with shorter notice. Understanding your rights as an employee, including the terms of your contract, your entitlement to paid leave and the process for resolving workplace disputes, is important from your first day of employment. Italian labour law provides strong protections for employees, but navigating the system requires awareness and, where needed, professional advice.

Italian Language Requirements for Immigration and Integration

Italian language proficiency is not technically required for all immigration routes to Italy, but it is practically essential for daily life, professional integration and long-term immigration goals. For work permits such as the Blue Card, there is no formal Italian language requirement: the application is assessed on your qualifications, your salary and the employer sponsorship. However, in practice, most professional roles in Italy require at least intermediate Italian proficiency, as business communication, client interactions and workplace culture are conducted primarily in Italian. For the study route, programmes taught in English do not require Italian, but your daily life outside the university will be significantly easier with at least basic Italian. For permanent residency and citizenship, Italian language proficiency is a formal requirement: you must demonstrate at least A2 level Italian for permanent residency and at least B1 level for citizenship.

Learning Italian before you arrive is the most effective strategy for integration, and there are several pathways available. Formal Italian language courses are offered by the Italian Cultural Institutes, the Dante Alighieri Society and various private language schools in major Pakistani cities. Online courses through platforms like Duolingo, Babbel and Coursera provide flexible learning options, though they should be supplemented with speaking practice through conversation groups or tutors. Some Italian universities offer preparatory Italian language courses for international students, which can be taken before or during your programme. Reaching A2 level within the first six months of arrival is a realistic goal for most learners, and reaching B1 within a year is achievable with consistent study and practice.

The Italian government offers free or subsidised Italian language courses for immigrants through the CPIA (Centri Provinciali per l Educazione degli Adulti) system. These adult education centres are located in most Italian cities and provide Italian language courses at various levels, from beginner to advanced. The courses are typically offered during the academic year and are open to all legal residents. Some CPIAs also offer courses specifically designed for immigrants, which focus on the language needed for workplace communication, interactions with government offices and daily life. Attending a CPIA course is not only a practical language learning step: it also demonstrates your commitment to integration, which is assessed when you apply for permanent residency or citizenship.

For Pakistani immigrants who speak Urdu, Punjabi or other Indo-Aryan languages, Italian shares some structural features that can facilitate learning. Both language families use subject-object-verb word order in certain contexts, and both have gendered nouns and verb conjugations. However, the Italian sound system, including vowel length and consonant clusters, is different from Urdu and Punjabi, and pronunciation requires focused practice. The written language is relatively straightforward for English speakers, as Italian spelling is largely phonetic and follows consistent rules. Combining formal study with daily immersion, including consuming Italian media, speaking with neighbours and colleagues and reading local newspapers, accelerates your progress significantly. The investment in Italian language proficiency is repaid many times over in your ability to navigate bureaucracy, build relationships and access opportunities that are unavailable to non-Italian speakers.

Italy Digital Nomad Visa and Self-Employment Routes

Italy introduced a digital nomad visa in 2024, and it represents a new immigration pathway that may be relevant for Pakistani professionals who work remotely for non-Italian employers. The digital nomad visa allows remote workers, freelancers and self-employed individuals to live and work in Italy for up to one year, with the possibility of renewal. To qualify, you must demonstrate that you have a remote employment contract or freelance clients outside Italy, that you have health insurance covering your stay and that you have sufficient financial resources to support yourself. The visa does not require a job offer from an Italian employer, which distinguishes it from the standard work permit routes, and it is not subject to the Decreto Flussi quota.

The self-employment route in Italy is another option for Pakistani immigrants who want to start a business or work as freelancers. The self-employment visa is included in the Decreto Flussi quota, which means it is subject to the annual quota limitation and the competitive click-day application process. To qualify, you must have a clear business plan, proof of financial resources and any professional qualifications required for your field of work. Some self-employment categories, such as writers, artists and researchers, have separate provisions that may be easier to access. The self-employment route requires registration with the Italian Chamber of Commerce, payment of social security contributions and compliance with Italian tax regulations, which adds a layer of administrative complexity compared to standard employment.

The digital nomad visa is particularly interesting for Pakistani professionals in technology, design, consulting and media, as it allows you to continue working for international clients or employers while living in Italy. The visa requires proof of remote work or freelance income, health insurance and accommodation in Italy. The application is submitted at the Italian consulate in your country of residence, and processing times vary. Once in Italy, you must register with the local immigration office and comply with Italian tax obligations on your worldwide income. The digital nomad visa is still relatively new, and the administrative details are evolving, so checking the latest requirements with the Italian consulate before applying is essential. For Pakistani professionals who are already working remotely, this visa provides a legal basis for living in Italy without needing to find an Italian employer or navigate the Decreto Flussi quota.

Combining the digital nomad or self-employment route with a long-term immigration strategy requires planning. The digital nomad visa is initially issued for one year and renewable, but it does not directly lead to permanent residency in the same way that a standard work permit does. If your goal is long-term settlement in Italy, you should plan to transition from a digital nomad visa to a standard work permit or Blue Card once you have established a professional presence in Italy. Building a client base in Italy, developing relationships with Italian businesses and demonstrating your value to the Italian economy are all steps that strengthen your position for a longer-term immigration route. The study-first route, followed by conversion to a work permit, remains the most reliable pathway for Pakistani immigrants who want to build a permanent life in Italy.

Building a Professional Network in Italy as a Pakistani Immigrant

Building a professional network in Italy is one of the most important steps you can take to secure employment, navigate bureaucracy and build a successful career as an immigrant. Unlike some countries where online job applications are the primary hiring mechanism, Italy relies heavily on personal connections and professional referrals. Many positions, particularly in smaller companies and professional services, are filled through personal networks before they are ever publicly advertised. This means that your ability to build and maintain professional relationships directly affects your employment prospects. Start building your network from your first day in Italy, whether you are there as a student, a worker or a job seeker.

LinkedIn is a practical starting point for professional networking in Italy. Create a complete and professional profile, connect with Italian professionals in your field, join relevant industry groups and engage with content that demonstrates your expertise and interest. Many Italian professionals are active on LinkedIn, and a well-crafted profile can attract attention from recruiters and potential employers. Beyond LinkedIn, professional associations and industry bodies in Italy often host events, workshops and conferences that provide opportunities to meet people in your field. Joining these associations, attending their events and participating in discussions demonstrates your commitment to the Italian professional community and creates opportunities for personal connections that online networking alone cannot replicate.

For Pakistani immigrants, community networks also play an important role in professional development. The Pakistani community in Italy, though smaller than in some other European countries, is present in cities like Milan, Rome and Bologna, and community organisations often facilitate professional connections between Pakistani professionals. These networks can provide introductions to Italian employers, advice on navigating the Italian workplace and support during the transition period. Combining community networking with professional networking creates a broader base of support and increases your chances of finding opportunities that match your skills and goals.

The Italian concept of network building is rooted in trust and reciprocity. Building a professional network is not about collecting business cards or LinkedIn connections: it is about developing genuine relationships based on mutual respect and shared professional interests. Be willing to help others in your network, share information and make introductions, and these gestures will be returned when you need support. Attend social events, accept invitations and invest time in getting to know your colleagues and contacts as people, not just as potential employers. This approach to networking takes time, but the relationships it produces are more durable and more likely to lead to meaningful professional opportunities.

faq.q: Can I get an Italian work visa without a degree?
faq.a: Yes. The EU Blue Card accepts five years of professional experience as equivalent to a higher-education qualification, especially for IT, engineering and senior management. The Decreto Flussi route also does not require a degree but is quota-capped.

faq.q: What is the difference between the EU Blue Card and Decreto Flussi?
faq.a: The Blue Card is quota-free, year-round and for qualified professionals above a salary threshold (about €35,500, or €28,200 in shortage sectors), with family work rights and faster processing. Decreto Flussi is the annual capped quota system for seasonal, trade and subordinate work.

faq.q: How long does the Italian Blue Card process take?
faq.a: About 2–4 months total: the Nulla Osta takes 30–90 days, then the Type D visa at the consulate, then conversion to the residence permit within 8 working days of arrival.

faq.q: Can my family live and work in Italy?
faq.a: Yes. EU Blue Card families get residence permits with immediate work rights, spouses can work without extra procedures, and children attend Italian public schools free. Family reunification also applies for spouses, minor children and dependent parents of residents.

faq.q: Can I switch from a tourist visa to a work visa in Italy?
faq.a: No. A Schengen C visa cannot be converted into a work or residence permit. You need a Nulla Osta obtained by your employer and a Type D work visa from an Italian consulate before you arrive. The main exception is converting a student permit to a work permit.

posts.title: New Zealand Student Visa: Fees & Requirements
posts.metaDescription: The 2026 New Zealand student visa: NZ$850 fee, NZ$20,000 living-cost requirement, documents, work rights and application timeline.
posts.excerpt: Everything about the 2026 New Zealand student visa, including the NZ$850 fee, the NZ$20,000/year funds requirement and 25 hrs/week work rights.
posts.bodyHtml:
The New Zealand student visa is one of the most affordable and most strategically useful in the developed world. In 2026 the fee-paying student visa costs NZD $850, the living-cost proof is NZD $20,000 per year, and a Level 7+ New Zealand degree plugs directly into the Skilled Migrant and Green List residence systems. That combination of low entry cost and a clear path to residency makes New Zealand a standout choice for students who want to stay after they graduate. This guide covers the fee, the funds you must prove, the documents, the work rights and the timeline.

New Zealand is genuinely small: eight universities, around 5.2 million people, and a tight housing market in Auckland, but the system is engineered to fast-track skilled graduates toward residence.

Key takeaways

  • The fee-paying student visa costs NZD $850 (Pathway Student Visa NZD $750), non-refundable.
  • You must prove NZD $20,000 per year for living costs (about $1,667 a month for stays under a year) plus tuition, return travel and insurance, with funds ideally held for three-plus months.
  • You need an Offer of Place from an NZQA-registered (approved) education provider and mandatory medical and travel insurance.
  • Tertiary students can work 25 hours a week during term and full-time in scheduled holidays; master's-by-research and PhD students can work unlimited hours.
  • Processing takes about 8 weeks, so apply around four months before your course starts (main intakes: February and July).
  • An NZ bachelor's earns 5 of the 6 Skilled Migrant points needed; an NZ master's can earn 5–6 outright, making the degree a direct route toward residence.

Visa fee and costs for 2026

The fee-paying student visa is NZD $850, and the Pathway Student Visa (for study plans with an approved pathway provider) is NZD $750. On top of the visa you must show evidence of funds for: first-year tuition, living costs of NZD $20,000 per year, return travel and health insurance (around NZD $500–855 a year). University tuition for international undergraduates runs roughly NZD 26,000–47,000 a year, while polytechnics start around NZD 9,000, and international PhD students pay domestic-rate fees (about NZD 7,500–9,000).

Documents you need

Start with the Offer of Place from an NZQA-approved provider, since everything flows from it. Then prepare proof of funds with a clear, traceable history, valid passport, a genuine-intention statement (reason for study and return plans), an English test if required (IELTS 6.0–6.5 is the typical university bar; 5.5–6.0 for polytechnics), medical and travel insurance, and, where needed, an x-ray or medical certificate. Biometrics are part of the application for most nationalities.

Work rights while studying

Tertiary students on a student visa can work up to 25 hours a week during term and full-time during scheduled holidays. Students in master's-by-research and PhD programs can work unlimited hours, and secondary students in Years 12–13 can work up to 20 hours a week with permission. The New Zealand minimum wage sits around NZD $23.50–23.95 an hour, so part-time work makes a real dent in living costs.

After graduation: staying in New Zealand

After study you can apply for the Post Study Work Visa (NZD $1,670): Level 7 degrees of 30+ weeks earn 1–3 years, and master's and PhD graduates get three years. A new 6-month Short-term Graduate Work Visa also launches on 16 November 2026. The migration payoff is the real story: an NZ bachelor's earns 5 of the 6 points in the Skilled Migrant system, an NZ master's can earn 5–6 outright, and NZ qualifications get a +1 point bonus over overseas ones from August 2026. Green List occupations (IT, engineering, health, construction) can go straight to residence. See our immigrate to New Zealand guide for the full points breakdown.

New Zealand Student Visa: Fees & Requirements: what this guide covers

This guide explains everything a Pakistani student needs to know about New Zealand student visa, including eligibility, costs, timelines and practical steps. Use the sections above to find the exact information you need, or bookmark this page and return as your application progresses.

Timeline and tips

Allow about 8 weeks for processing and apply around four months before your course starts, targeting the February or July intakes. Apply to an NZQA-approved provider early, because the Offer of Place gates everything else. For a fuller comparison of costs, universities and cities, see our study in New Zealand guide, and for country-by-country visa requirements, the visa guidance page.

New Zealand Student Visa Application Process Step by Step

The New Zealand student visa application is managed online through Immigration New Zealand website, and the process is designed to be straightforward for applicants who prepare their documents thoroughly before starting. The first step is to secure an offer of place from a New Zealand education provider that is approved to enrol international students. Your education provider will issue you with an offer of place document that includes your programme details, tuition fees and the start date. You will also need to pay a deposit toward your tuition, typically at least 50 percent of the first year fees, before your visa application can be processed. The education provider will send you a receipt for this payment, which you will include in your visa application.

The visa application itself is submitted online through the Immigration New Zealand portal. You will need to create an account, complete the application form and upload supporting documents, including your passport, offer of place, proof of tuition payment, evidence of financial capacity, health insurance documentation, police clearance certificates and academic transcripts. Financial capacity is one of the most important elements: you must demonstrate access to at least NZD 20,000 per year for living costs, plus the full amount of your tuition fees and return airfare. At the time of writing, these figures represent the minimum threshold, and Immigration New Zealand may ask for additional evidence if your financial situation is complex. The police clearance must be obtained from any country where you have lived for twelve months or more since turning seventeen.

Health requirements include a chest X-ray and, depending on your country of residence and the length of your intended stay, a full medical examination. For Pakistani applicants, a medical examination by an Immigration New Zealand panel physician is required, and the results are sent directly to Immigration New Zealand. The health check must be completed within three months of your visa application. You must also hold valid health insurance for the duration of your stay: your education provider may offer a group health insurance plan, or you can arrange your own cover through a New Zealand-based insurer, as long as it meets the minimum requirements set by Immigration New Zealand. The insurance must cover medical treatment, hospital care and repatriation.

Processing times for student visa applications from Pakistan vary, but at the time of writing, applications are typically processed within four to eight weeks if all documents are complete and no additional verification is required. Incomplete applications or those that require additional information can take significantly longer, so submitting a thorough and well-organised application is the single most effective way to avoid delays. Once approved, your visa will be issued as an electronic visa linked to your passport, and you will receive a notification email with your visa details. You should print a copy of this notification for your travel, although airlines can verify your visa status electronically. Plan to arrive in New Zealand no more than twenty-eight days before your programme starts, as your student visa permits early entry only within this window.

Acceptable Evidence of Funds for a New Zealand Student Visa

Demonstrating that you have sufficient funds is one of the most critical elements of a New Zealand student visa application, and Immigration New Zealand applies strict standards to what counts as acceptable evidence. The minimum requirement is NZD 20,000 per year for living costs, in addition to your full tuition fees for the duration of your programme and the cost of return airfare. For a two-year programme, this means you need to show access to at least NZD 40,000 for living costs, plus the total tuition amount, plus an estimated return airfare. The funds must be readily available to you, meaning they must be in a bank account, investment or financial instrument that can be accessed without significant restriction.

Acceptable forms of evidence include bank statements showing a consistent balance over a period of at least six months, a student loan approval letter from a recognised financial institution, a scholarship award letter that specifies the amount and duration of funding or a financial undertaking from a sponsor who is financially responsible for your studies. If you are relying on a sponsor, the sponsor must provide a statutory declaration or letter of support confirming their relationship to you and their commitment to funding your studies, along with evidence of their own financial capacity. Bank statements that show a sudden large deposit shortly before the application are likely to attract additional scrutiny, as Immigration New Zealand is looking for evidence that the funds have been available to you for a sustained period rather than borrowed temporarily to meet the visa requirement.

For Pakistani applicants, there are additional practical considerations. Bank statements from Pakistani banks are accepted, but they must be translated into English if they are in Urdu. The format should show the account holder name, account number, date of the statement and the balance in a currency that can be converted to New Zealand dollars. If your funds are held in multiple accounts, you can combine statements from different accounts to meet the threshold, but each account must be in your name or in the name of your sponsor. Scholarship letters from Pakistani government bodies, international organisations or universities should clearly state the total amount of funding, the duration and the conditions attached. If your scholarship covers tuition but not living costs, you will still need to show separate evidence of NZD 20,000 per year for your living expenses.

Immigration New Zealand may contact your bank or financial institution to verify the authenticity of your documents, so ensure that all information is accurate and that your bank is aware that a verification may come through. Do not provide altered, fabricated or misleading financial documents: this is a ground for visa refusal and can result in a ban on future applications. If your financial situation changes between submitting your application and receiving a decision, notify Immigration New Zealand immediately and provide updated evidence. The financial evidence requirement is not a formality: it is one of the most common reasons for visa delays and refusals, and it is worth investing time in getting it right before you submit.

Work Rights and Post-Study Work Visas in New Zealand

New Zealand offers some of the most generous work rights for international students in the developed world, and these rights extend beyond graduation into a post-study work visa that can lead directly to residence. While studying, you can work up to twenty hours per week during term time and full-time during scheduled breaks, such as summer and winter holidays. These work rights apply to students enrolled in programmes at NZQF level 7 or above (bachelor degrees and higher) at an approved education provider, and they are automatically included with your student visa. Part-time work during study is a practical way to reduce your living costs, gain New Zealand work experience and build professional connections that may help after graduation.

The Post-Study Work Visa (PSWV) is available to international students who complete an eligible qualification in New Zealand. At the time of writing, the PSWV allows graduates to work in New Zealand for a period of one to three years, depending on the level and duration of the qualification they completed. A bachelor degree or higher typically qualifies for a three-year open work visa, meaning you can work for any employer in any occupation. A postgraduate diploma or certain other qualifications may qualify for a two-year visa, and shorter qualifications may qualify for a one-year visa. The PSWV is an open visa, which means you are not tied to a specific employer, giving you the freedom to change jobs, pursue different career opportunities or start your own business during the visa period.

The transition from a PSWV to residence is one of New Zealand strongest draws. Graduates who work in occupations on the Green List, which includes roles in healthcare, engineering, construction, ICT and agriculture, can apply for residence through the Skilled Migrant Category or through a Green List-specific pathway. The specific requirements vary by occupation and change periodically, so check the Immigration New Zealand website for the current Green List before making career decisions. At the time of writing, some Green List roles offer a straight-to-residence pathway after two years of work in the role, while others require a two-year work period before residence can be applied for. Planning your study and career with the Green List in mind from the outset gives you the strongest chance of a smooth transition to residence.

For Pakistani students, the combination of affordable tuition, generous work rights and a clear post-study pathway makes New Zealand a strategically strong choice. The key is selecting a qualification and a field of study that align with both the Green List and your career goals. Before enrolling, research which occupations are on the Green List, which universities and polytechnics offer relevant programmes and what the employment landscape looks like in New Zealand for your field. Networking with New Zealand professionals in your industry, even before you arrive, through LinkedIn or professional associations, can help you understand the job market and make informed decisions about your programme of study. The work rights and post-study visa are valuable, but they are most valuable when they are part of a deliberate career strategy rather than a passive benefit.

Health Insurance Requirements for New Zealand Student Visa Holders

Health insurance is a mandatory requirement for all international students in New Zealand, and your student visa will not be granted without evidence of appropriate cover. Immigration New Zealand requires that your health insurance covers medical treatment, hospital care and repatriation for the full duration of your stay. The policy must be issued by a New Zealand-based insurer or an insurer that is recognised by Immigration New Zealand, and the coverage must meet the minimum standards specified in your visa conditions. At the time of writing, the minimum cover includes medical treatment for illness and accident, hospital accommodation and repatriation to your home country if medically necessary.

Many New Zealand education providers offer group health insurance plans for international students, which are designed to meet Immigration New Zealand requirements and are often the most convenient option. These plans are typically arranged through the university or polytechnic and are added to your tuition fees. The cost varies by provider and programme length, but at the time of writing, group plans for international students typically cost between NZD 500 and NZD 800 per year. Group plans have the advantage of being pre-approved by Immigration New Zealand, which eliminates the risk of your insurance not meeting the required standard. If you prefer to arrange your own insurance, you must ensure that the policy meets all Immigration New Zealand requirements and that you can provide a certificate of insurance in English with your visa application.

Understanding what your insurance covers, and what it does not, is important for managing your health and finances while in New Zealand. Most student health insurance plans cover doctor visits, hospital stays, emergency treatment and prescription medication, but they may not cover dental treatment, optical care or pre-existing conditions. Some plans have excess amounts (the amount you pay per claim before insurance coverage begins), and some limit the total amount payable per year. Read the policy document carefully before you commit to a plan, and if you have a specific health condition, confirm that it is covered or that you can arrange supplementary cover. New Zealand public healthcare system provides emergency treatment to everyone regardless of visa status, but ongoing treatment for international students is typically handled through private providers, which is why health insurance is essential.

If you hold a scholarship that includes health insurance, confirm with your scholarship provider that the cover meets Immigration New Zealand requirements. Some international scholarships provide health insurance through a global provider that may not be recognised by Immigration New Zealand, in which case you may need to supplement it with a New Zealand-based policy. The evidence of health insurance must be submitted with your visa application, and if you change your insurance provider after your visa is granted, you must ensure that the new policy continues to meet the visa conditions. Failure to maintain adequate health insurance throughout your stay can result in visa conditions being breached, which can affect future immigration applications. For Pakistani students who may be unfamiliar with New Zealand insurance system, the education provider international student office is a reliable first point of contact for guidance on suitable insurance options.

Dependent Visas and Bringing Family to New Zealand

If you are studying in New Zealand on a student visa and want to bring your partner or dependent children, New Zealand offers a straightforward dependent visa pathway. Your partner can apply for a partner of a student work visa, which allows them to work full-time in New Zealand for any employer for the duration of your student visa. Dependent children can apply for student or visitor visas, and if they are of school age, they can enrol in New Zealand schools. The dependent visa applications are linked to your student visa, so the validity of your partner and children visas is tied to the duration of your programme. This is a significant advantage for Pakistani students with families, as it allows your family to accompany you without the financial strain of separate visa applications and separate work rights for your partner.

To qualify for a dependent visa, you must demonstrate that your relationship with your partner is genuine and stable and that you have the financial capacity to support your family in New Zealand. Evidence of your relationship can include a marriage certificate, joint bank statements, shared accommodation records and photographs. If you are not married but are in a de facto relationship, you will need to provide evidence that you have been living together in a relationship similar to marriage for at least twelve months. Financial evidence for dependent visas is assessed in addition to your own financial evidence for the student visa, so you will need to show that you have sufficient funds to cover the living costs of your entire family. The minimum amount increases with each additional family member.

A practical consideration for families is the cost and availability of housing in New Zealand, particularly in Auckland, where the international student population is concentrated. Accommodation costs are a significant part of the family budget, and the New Zealand rental market can be competitive. University-owned student accommodation is typically designed for single students and may not be suitable for families, so most students with families rent privately. Looking for accommodation before you arrive, using university accommodation advisory services and connecting with Pakistani community groups in New Zealand can help you find suitable housing more quickly. Schools in New Zealand are generally of high quality, and dependent children of student visa holders can enrol in state schools, although fees may apply for international students at some schools. The education provider international student office can provide specific guidance on school enrolment for your children.

The ability of your partner to work full-time is one of the most valuable aspects of the dependent visa. Your partner income can significantly supplement your family finances while you study, and the work experience they gain in New Zealand contributes to their own professional development and to your family long-term immigration prospects. If your partner secures employment in an occupation on the Green List, this may strengthen your family overall position when you apply for residence after graduation. Discuss your family career goals and immigration strategy together before you leave Pakistan, so that both of you can make informed decisions about work, study and housing from the moment you arrive. The dependent visa pathway is designed to support families, but it works best when both partners approach the New Zealand experience as a shared project with coordinated goals.

New Zealand Student Visa Timeline and Pre-Departure Checklist

The New Zealand student visa timeline begins well before you submit your application, and working backwards from your programme start date ensures that you complete each step on time. The sequence is: secure an offer of place from a New Zealand education provider, pay your tuition deposit, gather all required documents (passport, academic transcripts, police clearances, financial evidence, health insurance, medical examination results), submit your visa application online, wait for processing, receive your electronic visa and book your travel. Each of these steps takes time, and delays in any one of them can push back your arrival. A realistic timeline begins at least four to five months before your programme start date, with the visa application submitted at least twelve weeks before you intend to travel.

Your pre-departure checklist should include several practical items that affect your experience from day one in New Zealand. Arrange your health insurance before you arrive, as the visa requires evidence of cover and you will need insurance from the moment you land. Research accommodation options and, if possible, arrange temporary housing for your first two weeks, whether through the university residential halls, a homestay or a short-term rental. Open a New Zealand bank account if your education provider offers this service before arrival, or plan to open one within your first week. Notify your education provider of your travel dates and arrival time so that they can arrange airport pickup or orientation support. Pack appropriate clothing for New Zealand weather, which varies significantly between the North and South Islands and between summer and winter. Bring copies of all important documents, including your visa notification, offer of place, insurance certificate and academic transcripts, both in physical and digital form.

Upon arrival in New Zealand, there are several administrative tasks that you must complete within your first weeks. Register with your education provider international student office, attend orientation and collect your student ID card. Register with a local doctor (GP) so that you can access healthcare when needed. If you plan to work while studying, confirm your work rights with your education provider and begin looking for part-time employment through university job boards, local newspapers or online platforms. Set up a mobile phone plan, as having a New Zealand phone number is important for opening bank accounts, renting accommodation and applying for jobs. Familiarise yourself with New Zealand road rules if you plan to drive, and with public transport options if you will be using buses or trains.

The transition to life in New Zealand is generally smooth for international students, but there are cultural differences worth understanding before you arrive. New Zealand culture values directness, punctuality and personal space, and the pace of life is generally more relaxed than in South Asian countries. The outdoors plays a significant role in New Zealand culture, and many social activities centre on hiking, sports and nature. New Zealand is a bicultural country with both Maori and European heritage, and understanding and respecting this bicultural identity is an important part of integration. The Pakistani community in New Zealand is growing, and Muslim community organisations, Halal food shops and mosques are available in major cities. Building a social network that includes both New Zealanders and fellow international students enriches your experience and helps you feel at home more quickly.

Choosing the Right Programme and Education Provider in New Zealand

New Zealand has eight universities, numerous polytechnics and institutes of technology, and several private training establishments, and choosing the right provider for your programme is one of the most important decisions you will make. All eight universities are ranked in the top three percent globally, and they each have particular strengths: the University of Auckland is strong in engineering, medicine and business; Victoria University of Wellington is known for law, humanities and public policy; the University of Canterbury excels in engineering and science; and the University of Otago is strong in health sciences and humanities. Polytechnics and institutes of technology, such as Otago Polytechnic and Wellington Institute of Technology, offer more vocationally oriented programmes with strong industry connections. The right choice depends on your career goals, your budget and the specific programme you want to study.

When evaluating programmes, look beyond the university ranking and examine the specific curriculum, the faculty expertise, the industry partnerships and the graduate outcomes. A programme that includes a work placement, industry project or practicum component provides practical experience that employers value, and it can significantly strengthen your post-study work prospects. Check whether the programme is accredited by the relevant professional body in New Zealand, particularly if you are studying in a regulated field such as engineering, nursing, teaching or accounting. Accreditation ensures that your qualification meets the standards required for professional registration in New Zealand, which is essential if you plan to work in a regulated profession after graduation.

The location of your education provider affects both your living costs and your social experience. Auckland, as New Zealand largest city, has the highest cost of living but also the widest range of employment opportunities and the largest international student community. Wellington, the capital, offers a vibrant cultural scene and strong government and public sector employment. Christchurch, Dunedin and Hamilton are smaller cities with lower costs of living and strong university communities. For Pakistani students, the availability of Halal food, mosques and a Pakistani community may be factors in choosing a city, and these resources are most readily available in Auckland and Wellington. Visiting the university website, attending virtual open days and connecting with current students through social media groups all help you make an informed decision about where to study.

Before you commit to a programme, verify that the education provider is approved by the New Zealand Qualifications Authority (NZQA) and that the programme is on the list of programmes approved for international student enrolment. Providers that are not NZQA-approved cannot enrol international students on student visas, and programmes that are not approved do not qualify for post-study work visas. This verification is essential: enrolling in a programme that does not meet these criteria can result in your visa being refused or your post-study work visa being denied. The Immigration New Zealand website maintains a list of approved providers and programmes, and you should cross-reference your chosen programme against this list before you accept an offer and pay your tuition deposit.

New Zealand Student Visa: Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them

The most common mistake in New Zealand student visa applications is submitting incomplete financial evidence. Immigration New Zealand requires specific documentation to prove that you have sufficient funds, and the evidence must meet strict criteria regarding format, time period and source. Bank statements that show a sudden large deposit, statements that are not in English, or evidence that does not clearly demonstrate access to the required amount will result in a request for additional information, which delays your application. To avoid this, begin building your financial evidence at least six months before you plan to submit your visa application, ensuring that your bank statements show a consistent and sufficient balance throughout this period.

A second common error is failing to provide adequate health insurance documentation. Immigration New Zealand requires evidence of health insurance that meets specific criteria, and many applications are delayed because the insurance policy provided does not clearly state the coverage details, the duration or the insurer recognition. Before you submit your visa application, verify that your health insurance policy explicitly states that it covers medical treatment, hospital care and repatriation for the full duration of your stay, and that the insurer is recognised by Immigration New Zealand. If your education provider offers a group health insurance plan, this is often the simplest option, as it is pre-approved and meets all requirements.

Police clearance certificates are another area where delays occur. You must provide a police clearance from any country where you have lived for twelve months or more since turning seventeen, and obtaining these certificates can take several weeks, particularly if you have lived in multiple countries. Begin the process of obtaining police clearances as soon as you decide to apply for a New Zealand student visa, as the certificates are typically valid for a limited period and must be current at the time of your visa application. If you have lived in Pakistan for the past several years, the Pakistani police clearance is the primary document you need, and it can be obtained from the regional police office in the city where you reside.

Finally, many applicants underestimate the importance of the statement of purpose or study plan that accompanies their visa application. While New Zealand does not require a formal essay, a clear and concise explanation of why you chose New Zealand, why you chose your specific programme and what you plan to do after graduation strengthens your application and demonstrates that you are a genuine student. This statement should be one to two pages, written in clear English, and should connect your academic background to your career goals and to the specific programme you have chosen. Taking the time to write a thoughtful statement is a small investment that can make a meaningful difference in the outcome of your application.

Official sources and references

  • gov.uk — official information and resources.
  • travel.state.gov — official information and resources.

NZ student visa vital stats

New Zealand student visa essentials at a glance.
